EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Sat, 24 Oct 2026 07:54:52 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Calls mount for UN World Food Programme, which feeds over a million people in Gaza, to quit contract with Palantir https://euobserver.com/244723/calls-mount-for-un-world-food-programme-which-feeds-1-4m-people-in-gaza-to-quit-contract-with-palantir/ Sat, 24 Oct 2026 09:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244723 The UN food agency helping Palestinians and others in need across the world has come under scrutiny for its contract with Palantir –  the controversial US tech and AI company used by various international border police and militaries to sort data and better identify targets.]]> The UN food agency helping Palestinians and others in need across the world has come under scrutiny for its contract with Palantir –  the controversial US tech and AI company used by various international border police and militaries to sort data and better identify targets.

The UN’s food agency, the World Food Programme (WFP), prolonged its contract with Palantir in July, prompting civil organisations to urge the end of these agreements in a letter published on Friday (23 October).

Some 3,000 European citizens have written to the WFP’s leadership, calling for the agency to end its Palantir partnership.

The WFP holds one of the biggest biometric databases in the world, with millions of its records containing information about vulnerable populations.

Read more

Public money for Palantir, pennies back in tax: EU procurement is failing Europe

WFP is effectively supporting a company that undermines its own operations in Palestine by helping kill civilians for another client, which is “a very strong contradiction,”  Giulio Carini, head of campaigns at an NGO WeMove Europe told EUobserver.

“On one hand, you’re feeding people of Gaza, but then, on the other hand, you’re using software that is being used also to kill [them],” he added.

As many as 1.1 million people are reached by the WFP in Gaza each month, out of the 1.4 million facing acute food insecurity. The organisation is complaining that it had to scale down its food assistance in Gaza and the West Bank due to a lack of funding.

The WFP has argued that its use of Palantir’s software to compile its datasets and make better decisions has saved them $50m [€45m] that would otherwise be spent on inefficient management of its resources.

]]> [Interview] Bulgaria’s presidential election becomes a test of Rumen Radev’s grip on power https://euobserver.com/244554/interview-bulgarias-presidential-election-becomes-a-test-of-rumen-radevs-grip-on-power/ Sat, 24 Oct 2026 07:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244554 Bulgaria holds its presidential election on Sunday. A moment to decide whether to consolidate power around the current prime minister - prioritising stability over institutional balance.]]> Incumbent president Iliana Yotova is leading Bulgaria’s 2026 presidential election race, alongside her running mate, Kiril Vulchev, securing 47.3 percent support among likely voters, according to a poll released on Wednesday (21 October).

Andrei Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister, and his running mate, Georgi Kandev, rank second with around 30 percent. Leaving the pro-Russian Kostadin Kostadinov and Petar Volgin is in third place on just over ten percent.

Bulgaria is voting on Sunday (25 October) and the vote can be seen as “a test of the government’s stability”, according to Ivaylo Iliev, a political scientist, with whom we analyse Bulgarian presidential elections in three points.

1. A test of the government’s stability

The election could consolidate political influence around prime minister Rumen Radev, or expose the limits of his camp’s support.

The PM’s Progressive Bulgaria, which secured a parliamentary majority in April 2026, is facing criticism over its budget plans and handling of security threats. Recent attacks on merchant vessels in the Black Sea have raised questions about Bulgaria’s ability to protect its interests and reassure its allies.

Read more

EU unlikely to send Black Sea naval mission to repel Russian drone attacks on Ukrainian grain ships, despite Kallas’ support

Iotova, who served as Radev’s vice-president for nine years, is closely associated with the prime minister. And her victory could be interpreted as an endorsement of the governing camp.

“Radev has his candidate in these elections and he is obviously the favourite to win a second round,” Iliev says.

However, the Black Sea attacks have “definitely negatively affected both” Iotova’s campaign and public confidence in the government’s security response, he adds.

The government’s response, alongside its nuanced position on Russia’s war against Ukraine, may appeal to voters sceptical of confrontation with Moscow. At the same time, it also risks complicating Bulgaria’s relations with its European and Nato partners.

“Radev demonstrates two different types of behaviour”, says Iliev.

On the domestic front, he is “balanced”, “vague” or even “without specifics”, Iliev says. For Radev does not want “to cause discontent among his pro-Russian voters”.

On the foreign policy however, Radev is more seeking to get as close as possible to the European consensus, but “with a minimal effort.”

2. Taking the government to account?

The second question is whether the presidency can act as a counterweight to the executive or will reinforce the same centre of political influence.

Gyurov’s campaign has warned against putting “all the eggs in one basket”. Concentrating power around Radev and Iotova could weaken independent scrutiny he says.

A Gyurov victory could give the presidency a more “independent voice”, says Iliev.

However, institutional checks and balances do not necessarily translate into electoral support.

]]> [Interview] Ousting Netanyahu won’t curb right-wing Israeli nationalism, says expert ahead of Tuesday’s Knesset elections https://euobserver.com/243681/interview-removing-netanyahu-wont-curb-right-wing-israeli-nationalism-says-expert-ahead-of-tuesdays-knesset-elections/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:22:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243681 Beth Oppenheim, fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, explains how a shift in Israeli society will shape voting on 27 October. Her analysis groups Israeli political forces into liberal Zionists, nationalists, religious nationalists, and ultra-Orthodox factions.]]> First published in Deník N.

Even if Israelis vote out the current government, an ideological shift will endure, says Beth Oppenheim, a policy fellow in the Middle East and North Africa programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations.

The London-based analyst explains how once-fringe ideas have crept into the political mainstream and the limitations of liberalism.

In this interview:

  • Why Netanyahu’s departure would not bring about fundamental change.
  • How 7 October has put diplomacy permanently off the table.
  • What to expect if a new government was elected in Knesset (Israeli parliament) elections.
  • The lessons Europe can draw from all this.

You say Israel’s illiberal and ethnonationalist turn represents a transformation beyond Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu; these ideologies would not disappear even with him gone. In your analysis of Israeli politics, you avoid the traditional left–right political spectrum – why?

Beth Oppenheim: In the Ideas of Israel project for ECFR, I wanted to unpack this binary we often see on the question of Netanyahu’s leadership. He dominates Israeli politics, but the debate about the prime minister often obscures more interesting trends like the rightward shift of Israeli politics. Often, the opposition is referred to as the liberal bloc, whom the right wing label as leftists – but this is inaccurate.

The pro-Netanyahus form a government coalition, while the opposition bloc is actually rather ideologically diverse. So in my research I wanted to go beyond the reductive question of Netanyahu to understand how parties behave in elections; I wanted to see where all these different parties’ ideologies and visions fit in. 

And this led you to categorise Israeli parties into four groups: the liberal Zionists, the nationalists, the ultra-Orthodox camp, and the religious nationalists. Could you describe each group? Let’s start with the liberal Zionists, who are considered the most left-wing of the Jewish Israeli camps…

Of course. The liberal Zionists include figures such as Yair Golan, Yair Lapid and Gadi Eisenkot.

Eisenkot (Yashar party) is a former general in the military. Despite this, many on the right brand him as a leftist. 

Lapid (Yesh Atid party) comes from a liberal centrist tradition in the mould of his father. Like Eisenkot, he is very secular. A secular vision for Israel and an emphasis on liberal democratic institutions unite the camp of liberal Zionists.

Golan (The Democrats party) is the left flank of this camp. In Europe, he wouldn’t be seen as far left, but within the Israeli spectrum, he is seen as radical. He has security credentials, too, but he’s the only liberal Zionist who talks about a political settlement with the Palestinians. 

The two-state solution is not really on the menu in the Jewish Israeli political mainstream – that’s now the preserve of the far-left fringe; it’s not a mainstream discussion anymore. 

“The two-state solution is not really on the menu in the Jewish Israeli political mainstream”

The liberal Zionists are united around their secularism and their commitment to the liberal democratic institutions, but there’s one big caveat: when it comes to the Palestinian issue, their liberalism is more circumscribed. 

They are not talking about the ongoing occupation and the effect that that has on Israel’s democratic standing. But of course, they’re very united in their opposition to Netanyahu.

The liberal Zionist camp lacks a coherent platform other than this; they basically advocate for good governance, but don’t offer a robust vision. 

And that cannot be said about the nationalists, whose vision is quite clear, right?

Traditionally, the nationalist camp was the mainstream right wing. Today’s main contenders are prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu.

Meanwhile, former prime minister Naftali Bennett is running on a joint list with Lapid’s Yesh Atid, called Beyachad (‘Together’). Bennett and Lapid joined forces despite coming from different ideological traditions. They have very different ideas about the country, but they’re coming together to present a more technocratic agenda, get Netanyahu out and normalise Israeli politics. 

Read more

EU risks funding Israeli firms which help develop NAZA-type violent tech

The nationalist camp descends from the Revisionist Zionist tradition based on Ze’ev Jabotinsky’s vision: a liberal democratic outlook fused with ultra-nationalist convictions. So to take a Revisionist Zionist view is to take a hawkish and hardline approach towards Arabs, while keeping a commitment to liberal democratic values. But affinity for liberalism and democratic values has really withered away over recent decades, not only under Netanyahu.

And then there is the ultra-Orthodox camp, without which the current government would never have completed a full term.

The ultra-Orthodox group does not fit easily on the left-to-right political spectrum, which in the Israeli understanding is defined by hawkishness on Palestinians and security.

They are made up of two Ashkenazi parties – Degel HaTorah and Agudat Yisrael – and Sephardic party Shas. What unites them is strict religious observance of Jewish law and their commitment to separation from secular society or modernity.

“The ultra-Orthodox camp is predominantly non-Zionist, but not necessarily anti-Zionist”

Interestingly, the ultra-Orthodox camp is predominantly non-Zionist, but not necessarily anti-Zionist since they didn’t endorse the creation of Israel in its secular form. They engage with the state, but in a limited way – they’re very transactional and pragmatic.

And the ultra-orthodox camp work within state apparatus to advance sectoral interests, yeshiva education, the military service exemption, and subsidies to maintain a somewhat introverted separation from the rest of society.

They are mostly passive when it comes to issues of foreign policy and security policy, but they do not support loss of Jewish life for nationalist ends – they don’t believe that the state in its current form is sacred. And so they don’t, for instance, endorse the loss of Jewish life for territorial expansion.

Read more

No Israeli bonds on sale in EU for now, in de facto €2.2bn sanction

That leaves us with the last category: the religious nationalist camp.

Religious nationalists draw together ultra-orthodox religious observance, but with ultra-nationalism.

]]> Moscow elites pleased with US envoy Witkoff and far from agreeing to peace (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,702) https://euobserver.com/244704/moscow-elites-pleased-with-us-envoy-witkoff-and-far-from-agreeing-to-peace-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1702/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:07:29 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244704 Starshield, the defense version of Starlink, seems to remain slow despite US assurances that it was fully back. And journalists from Russia reveal what is being discussed by Kremlin and US officials as they seek a deal on Ukraine.]]>
  • Russian journalists reveal what the Kremlin and US are discussing.
  • Starshield was supposedly fixed, but that doesn’t seem to be the case.
  • Russians advance in Rai-Oleksandrivka towards Sloviansk.
  • Russia loses two combat Sukhoi aircraft in accidents in one day.
  • Map of the day: Rai-Oleksandrivka
  • Videos of the day: Kramatorsk evacuation; Russian Su-30 crashes; how helicopters hunt drones.

    • Russian journalists have described the nature of talks between the Kremlin and the US. A demilitarised zone in Donbas. A Ukraine without Nato membership but is allowed to join the EU membership in return. Sanctions against Russia eased, Russian gas in Europe and news talks on the Nord Stream 2 pipeline. And America makes its own deals with Russia.

    This is how, according to The Economist, the US proposal to the Kremlin for ending the war sounded, presented in Moscow on Wednesday (21 October) by Steve Witkoff, Trump’s negotiator.

    It sounds like something Russia might welcome, but that does not appear to be the case. At least not according to the findings of the Russian exile website Verstka, which a day later published an extensive report on the mood among Russia’s Kremlin-linked elite.

    The article, signed by the newspaper’s editorial board, contains numerous quotes from government officials and people close to the regime, whose views on the prospect of swiftly reaching a peace deal and ending the fighting are sceptical.

    Verstka wrote that war fatigue was mounting among these people, whose names it naturally did not disclose, but that they fully defer to Russian president Vladimir Putin and are waiting to see what he agrees with US president Donald Trump.

    “It can be said with certainty that American sympathies have shifted to our side. We have been working on this for a year and a half,” a source close to the foreign ministry told the journalists, describing Moscow’s strategy.

    Russia achieved this through the following argument: since Ukraine considers itself a victim — which it undoubtedly is, editor’s note — and asks for assistance, but is unwilling to make concessions in return for that assistance, it is no longer in fact a victim, but a player with ambitions of its own, which Western taxpayers are unwilling to fund.

    Incidentally, the Slovak government uses very similar rhetoric and arguments.

    According to the same source, Moscow will emphasise during the talks the hopelessness of Ukraine’s supposed situation.

    Another quoted voice was a political strategist directly linked to the Kremlin, who pointed out that Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner did not directly take part in the talks in St Petersburg on 21 October, reportedly due to illness.

    Nevertheless, this source also praised the US approach, even if Trump’s dispute with Ukraine proved only short-lived: “We have nothing to lose from these solutions. And we could gain both an improved budget and an advantage on the battlefield.” At the same time, the domestic political strategist saw no fundamental changes that could lead to an end to the fighting.

    The extent of the irrationality prevailing within the regime was illustrated by statements from another unnamed representative of a formally non-governmental organisation working directly with the Kremlin.

    In his analysis, he claimed that Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky had created a dictatorial system from which neither elections nor a coup could remove him, and that the war would not end while he remained in office. He also cited reports by Russia’s foreign intelligence service claiming that Kyiv was cooperating with Mexican drug cartels.

    Another government official had low expectations of the Americans: “For almost two years now, we have been saying that Trump is supposedly one of us and that the talks are constructive, but they have produced no results. We are fighting, burning, drowning, suffering alongside our homeland.”

    The man spoke of a “peace wing”, allegedly comprising people in the presidential administration responsible for domestic policy and economic circles, but this did not mean that there was any open opposition to the war.

    “There is no escape from the ship. We are waiting for them to have had enough of the war,” the official said.

    ]]>         New EU-wide asylum law ends up in court in Italy https://euobserver.com/244651/new-eu-wide-asylum-law-ends-up-in-court-in-italy/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 14:22:27 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244651 An Egyptian national who sought protection in Italy after arriving on the island of Lampedusa in August may end up dealing a constitutional blow to the EU's asylum laws after seeking legal counsel. ]]> An Egyptian national who sought protection in Italy after arriving on the island of Lampedusa in August may end up dealing a constitutional blow to the EU’s asylum laws after seeking legal counsel.

    The Egyptian, who is not named, had his asylum claim rejected even though he did not understand his translator. His is appealing.

    “Not even European Union law can conflict with our supreme principles,” his lawyer, Claudia Avenia told EUobserver earlier this week.

    Aside from his own personal circumstances, his legal case is raising serious issues that could have a knock-on effect on the EU’s new asylum and migration pact, which kicked into force this past June across all 27 EU member states.

    Because he is from Egypt, he was shuffled through a fast track asylum procedure. EU laws require the accelerated process from nationals who have a 20 percent chance or less of getting asylum in Europe. Egypt fits into this category.

    A new EU law also meant that he was technically not yet legally inside the EU as authorities carried out health checks, identification and other assessments during a so-called pre-screening phase.

    It means he was banned from stepping outside a reception centre, where he was being housed.

    Lawyers describe it as the legal fiction of non-entry, similar in scope to certain areas of international airports. Rights experts had earlier warned, when the EU rules were being drafted, that this would lead to defacto detention.

    French push for legal limbos on EU borders

    “EU external decisions have direct consequences for Jews living in Europe. Diplomats should hear from the person who sees those consequences every day,” said Pinchas Goldschmidt, who heads the Conference of European Rabbis (CER) in Munich, Germany.

    The European Jewish Congress (EJC) in Brussels also told EUobserver: “The [EU antisemitism] coordinator should ensure that this objective is systematically reflected in all relevant EU policies, including external action and foreign policy.”

    They spoke as von Schnurbein prepared to leave her EU post after 10 years to become a German “federal government commissioner for Jewish life in Germany and the fight against antisemitism” on 28 October.

    The 53-year-old German baroness was highly active at events in EU capitals, had three staff, and travelled to Israel, Serbia, Switzerland, and the US.

    She also worked next door to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and had close ties with the Israeli government.

    ]]>         Big fish hooked in Hungary, as Orbán’s ex-bank chief placed in custody (Day 163 of the Tisza government) https://euobserver.com/244500/big-fish-hooked-in-hungary-as-orbans-ex-bank-chief-placed-in-custody-day-163-of-the-tisza-government/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 13:09:54 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244500 Prosecutors are circling Orbán’s ex‑bank chief, as Magyar rewrites Hungary’s budget.]]> The series continues as we report on developments following April’s historic election and on the steps taken since then by the Tisza government. This week, we cover the following topics:

    • Orbán’s former right-hand man in custody.
    • What did we learn from Tisza’s first budget?
    • Ursula von der Leyen to give a speech on the anniversary of the revolution.
    • Poll of the week: more than four million people back Tisza.

    Orbán’s ex-right-hand man in custody

    The last time a central bank governor was taken into custody in Hungary was in 1944, during the German occupation, as Válasz Online pointed out. This 82-year hiatus ended on Wednesday (21 October), when György Matolcsy was taken into police custody.

    But Matolcsy is not simply a former central bank governor; he is one of the architects of Orbán’s economic policy, a key figure in the former prime minister’s system, and together with his family he has in recent years become one of the symbols of Fidesz’s taste for luxury.

    Who is György Matolcsy?

    “I have a very strong emotional relationship with Matolcsy. I owe him a great deal, I have learned a great many things from him. Matolcsy is an economist of historic stature,” prime minister Péter Magyar quoted ex-prime minister Viktor Orbán’s words from an interview last November, after the former central bank governor had been taken into custody.

    Matolcsy was a member of the Hungarian Socialist Workers’ Party (MSZMP), and after the regime change he became prime minister József Antall’s chief adviser. In 1999 he joined Orbán’s advisory board, and from 2000 to 2002 he served as economy minister in the first Orbán cabinet.

    Even after the 2002 election defeat he remained loyal to Orbán, and in 2010 he became minister for national economy, meaning he was put in charge of both the finance and economy portfolios at the head of a merged super-ministry. It was at this time that Orbán called him his right-hand man.

    Matolcsy was the architect of Orbán’s “unorthodox economic policy”; he oversaw the nationalisation of private pension funds, the sending home of the IMF from Hungary, and the introduction of high sectoral surtaxes.

    The great bank heist

    He was appointed central bank governor in 2013, and by 2016 the foundations scandal had already broken. It emerged that 266bn forints’ worth (€840m) of public assets had been shifted into the foundations of the Hungarian National Bank (MNB). These foundations bought buildings and works of art, and also granted substantial benefits to their own leaders.

    Later, the foundations’ money was entrusted to an asset management company, which obtained further funds and thus came to control assets of around 500bn forints, of which some 400bn forints (€1bn) – was public money.

    This asset manager built up an international corporate network, behind which stood the central bank governor’s son, Ádám Matolcsy, and his circle. So why are we still changing the clocks?

    On Sunday (25 October), Europeans will once again turn their clocks back by one hour. The familiar ritual will again raise the same question: did the European Union not decide years ago to end seasonal clock changes?

    The question entered the European agenda largely from the bottom up.

    Citizens repeatedly contacted and petitioned the European Parliament, raising concerns about health, sleep disruption and the continuing usefulness of changing the clocks twice a year.

    A citizens’ initiative presented to the Finnish Parliament in 2017 gave the issue further momentum. Finland could not end the practice alone because it was regulated at EU level.

    On 8 February 2018, the European Parliament called on the EU Commission to assess the existing directive and, if necessary, propose its revision.

    84% public support for ending clock changes…

    The commission subsequently launched a public consultation. It received approximately 4.6 million responses from citizens, the highest number ever recorded for an EU consultation at that time. Among those who participated, 84 percent supported ending the twice-yearly clock changes.

    The consultation was not a referendum, and participation varied considerably between member states. Nevertheless, millions of Europeans sent a clear political message.

    Jean-Claude Juncker highlighted the issue in his 2018 State of the Union address. Shortly afterwards, the commission proposed ending seasonal clock changes while allowing each member state to choose permanent summer time or permanent standard time.

    …and MEPs agree

    In March 2019, the European Parliament approved the proposal in plenary by 410 votes to 192, with 51 abstentions. The final clock change was expected in 2021.

    Yet 2021 came and went, and Europeans continued adjusting their clocks every March and October.

    Parliament has not reversed its position, and the commission has not formally withdrawn its proposal. The file remains blocked because member state governments have never agreed on a common position in the Council.

    No simple solution for 27 states

    Ending the clock change sounds simple until governments must decide what replaces it. Should countries remain permanently on summer time or standard time? What happens if neighbouring countries make different choices? How would a patchwork of time zones affect transport, aviation, trade and the single market?

    These are legitimate questions.

    A poorly coordinated decision could create new problems while solving the old one. Some governments also requested a more detailed assessment of the consequences. The pandemic and the crises that followed then pushed the issue further down the political agenda.

    However, the crisis cannot explain indefinite inaction. Eight years after the Commission presented its proposal, the Council has still not adopted a position. Without it, negotiations with Parliament cannot move towards a final agreement.

    This is where a practical question about clocks becomes a problem of democracy, accountability and political communication.

    Citizens were encouraged to participate. Millions did. Parliament responded adequately. The commission presented the consultation as evidence that Europe was listening. Its president announced that clock-changing would stop, and Parliament endorsed the proposal with a clear majority.

    Then the process got  stuck.

    Twice a year, Europeans are reminded of this promise, but receive little to no explanation about who is blocking progress, which governments support which option or how the disagreement might be resolved.

    Simply saying that “the EU failed” would, however, hide who has the concrete political responsibility. The EU is a complex, multilevel decision-making system in which responsibility is shared among different institutions and member state governments. Parliament adopted its position, while national capitals failed to agree in the council.

    Those governments should explain their positions instead of allowing “Brussels” to absorb the blame like often happens, for their collective indecision.

    The European Commission also has certain responsibility because her proposed legislation left the most difficult question, the choice of permanent time, to individual countries. 

    In any case, the EU risks turning, or did turn,  an example of successful citizen agenda-setting into an example of participatory failure.

    The issue may not be Europe’s most urgent challenge right now, but credibility and a positive image is also built through implementation of citizens’ demands such as this one.

    People notice when a widely announced change does not happen, especially when it impacts directly and negatively their daily life. They also notice when nobody explains why.

    Member state governments should state publicly whether they favour permanent summer time, permanent standard time or retaining the current system. The council should put the issue back on its agenda and strive to achieve an agreement.

    And if this is not possible, Europeans deserve a clear explanation why their participation led nowhere.

    Once they reach their offices, they meet the same industry again, this time in person. The seven biggest oil and gas companies alone have declared lobbying budgets of almost €64m.

    Fossil Free Politics research shows EU Commissioners and their cabinets had nearly 900 meetings with fossil fuel lobbyists in the last term. That’s nearly once every working day, showing just how embedded the industry is in the daily rhythm of Brussels life.

    Some files come under particularly heavy pressure, with one egregious example being how a secretive alliance of eleven large multinational enterprises worked to tear down the EU’s flagship human rights and climate law last year, the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD).

    Read more

    MEPs vote in favour of major rollback of corporate sustainability laws

    The fossil fuel industry is currently mounting an extremely intense lobbying campaign to delay and dilute the EU Methane Emissions Regulation over the past year.

    Over 80 percent of all commission meetings with external interest representatives on this regulation involved fossil fuel lobbyists, and the European Parliament is no better. All 17 MEPs who called for the methane regulation to be reopened in an April 2026 letter to the commission had met with fossil fuel lobbyists in the preceding year.

    And those are only the declared figures.

    Lobbyists roaming the corridors

    Safe to say, the real total is almost certainly higher. According to new research by Reclaim Finance, on two out of every three days, the fossil-fuel lobbyists present at the European Parliament had no meetings scheduled with MEPs. They roam the corridors and cafés in the building, aiming to bump into the MEPs they wish to influence.

    The councillors behind these fossil ad ban motions are not pretending that a few billboards will single-handedly solve the climate crisis, but they refuse to continue letting public spaces be misused by the fossil, automotive and aviation industry to freely promote their propaganda; as for the latter, especially since the advertised destinations are often precisely those places that have been the victims of severe climate disruptions..  

    “The summer of 2026 was a painful awakening to the harsh reality of the consequences of the climate crisis,” said Mathias Gyselen, the Ecolo-Groen councillor who tabled Schaerbeek’s motion in September.

    “Heatwaves, heat islands and heat deaths are unfortunately becoming the new normal in the city. Doing nothing is no longer an option.”

    They are right. Advertising is how the fossil fuel industry keeps its social licence, presenting itself as part of the solution while expanding the very products driving the crisis.

    Not just the five sub-municipalities of the Brussels capital acknowledge this, but over 70+ cities worldwide have taken steps to clear their streets from fossil fuel advertising, among them Amsterdam, Sydney, Stockholm and Edinburgh.

    The problems with advertisements, and multi-million euro lobby strategies, are not just that they very much harm the planet, they are also fundamentally undemocratic. 

    Residents, community groups and civil society organisations cannot match the industry’s firepower. They do not have the budgets, the staff or the open doors that put them across the table from lawmakers week after week.

    Europe has dealt with this before.

    ‘Godfathers of climate chaos’

    Tobacco lobbyists no longer get privileged access to health ministers, nor can cigarette brands buy billboards. For many similar reasons the world wants to end fossil fuels, the EU banned tobacco advertising because promoting a deadly product was incompatible with public health.

    UN secretary-general António Guterres made the same comparison in 2024 when he urged every country to ban fossil fuel advertising, naming fossil-fuel companies as the “godfathers of climate chaos”

    Municipal motions are not binding, so the decision now lies with the Brussels-Capital Region, which controls advertising in the metro, along regional roads and on its own infrastructure. A first obvious step is that it should listen to its municipalities and introduce a city-wide ban.

    But the message is also addressed to the institutions on the other side of the Rue de la Loi.

    If the streets of Europe’s capital are being cleared of fossil fuel promotion, the corridors of its institutions should be too. That means limiting the industry’s access to decision-makers, closing the revolving door, and rejecting fossil fuel sponsorship and partnerships, just as the EU did with tobacco.

    The municipalities of Brussels have shown what local democracy looks like. Now it is up to the region and the EU institutions to show that Europe’s capital is not for sale; not on its billboards, and not in its corridors of power.

    ]]>         Serbia’s election: can a student-led movement of hope overcome Vučić’s hollowed-out political system? https://euobserver.com/244185/serbias-election-can-a-student-led-movement-of-hope-overcome-vucics-hollowed-out-political-system/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 09:18:43 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244185 Sunday’s vote could reshape the country’s political future. But even a breakthrough for the student movement would leave a deeper question: can democratic change take root in institutions that protesters say have been hollowed out?]]> For years, Serbia’s opposition has struggled to turn public discontent into a credible challenge to Aleksandar Vučić’s political dominance. On Sunday (25 October), a student-led movement that began with demands for accountability after a deadly train station collapse will attempt to do what established opposition forces have repeatedly failed to achieve: translate civic mobilisation into political change.

    The upcoming parliamentary elections are about more than the (re)distribution of seats. They represent the endeavour citizens want and need in a democratic society.

    For several years now, “the students operate according to the principles of direct democracy,” senior research associate at the University of Belgrade, Vasiljević told EUobserver. They gather in “plenums” and make collective decisions.

    The motor behind that movement was anger. The lack of accountability after the collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station on 1 November 2024, which killed 16 people was the main trigger.

    Read more

    Why is the EU ignoring Serbia’s student protests?

    Since then, protests have been taken place around in the country. Eventually, they grew into a nationwide challenge to the government. The student movement even marched from Belgrade to Brussels and Strasbourg to appeal to the EU institutions.

    “It brought some irreversible changes that will have a lasting impact on society,” said Vasiljević.

    And these changes could be now transposed into politics. “The country has been held captive for far too long by one ruling party and, in fact, one ruling elite,” Miloje Savić, a volunteering poll observer, told EUobserver.

    For many Serbs, as for Savić, the students’ organisation represent “a tectonic shift in how society is organised and how it should function.”

    The Student List, now the electoral vehicle for the mobilisation, has given people frustrated with established politics a new focus for their demands. The main idea being that political participation can be rebuilt from the ground up.

    “It is not a good time to be living in Serbia. And during my life, I can’t remember a time when it was,” Ivan Bartoš, a 31-year-old organiser of student protests in Bački Petrovac told EUobserver.

    Serbia, as many European countries, is suffering from an ageing population. It brings to the social debate a generational difference. On one side, the middle-aged and “corrupted” regime led by Vučić, on the other, a proposal of change without real political experience.

    Read more

    MEPs call for tougher line on Serbia as rule-of-law problems stall membership talks

    And the question that is heard in the run-up to the elections is “does Serbia need a professional politician who has been trained for years in kleptocracy, or is society willing to take a risk?”

    Vučić’s ‘men in black’?

    Yet the movement’s rise has exposed a fundamental tension: society may be changing faster than the institutions through which change must be delivered.

    “The institutions have been captured and controlled by the regime. There is not enough institutional space to accommodate these political changes,” Vasiljević said.

    Previous Serbian elections have been accompanied by allegations of vote-buying, voter intimidation and ballot-box stuffing. After the last ones, held in December 2023, European MP’s called for “independent investigations into the irregularities”.

    Knowing what is at stake, the Student List is trained an unprecedented number of poll monitors (15,000), seeking to protect the vote and document potential irregularities.

    Attacks on opposition representatives by groups of unidentified men dressed in black have repeatedly raised concerns during the rule of Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

    The media are not safe either.

      <title>Trump drops some Canada tariffs in bid to boost embattled Susan Collins in Maine</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/susan-collins-maine-trump-tariffs-canada</link>
      <description><p>Republican senator faces critical re-election battle in state where president’s trade war has outraged voters </p><p>Donald Trump dropped some of the US’s tariffs on Canada on Friday to “better serve the public interest” the White House said, handing a win to Susan Collins, the embattled Republican senator for Maine, as she faces a tight re-election campaign that will help determine whether Democrats can flip control of Congress.</p><p>Collins announced that the exemptions would apply to nine agricultural products, including blueberries, potatoes, apples and seaweed. She added that many of the state’s farmers rely on specialized equipment and materials from across the border that are “unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/susan-collins-maine-trump-tariffs-canada">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/y2k-used-cars-gen-z</link>
      <description><p>People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans</p><p>Jack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.</p><p>Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/y2k-used-cars-gen-z">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Judge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for deposition</p><p>Donald Trump has been ordered by a US judge to cooperate with the discovery process mandated for his lawsuit against the BBC and to sit for a deposition by 11 December – or else he could be subject to sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the $10bn lawsuit.</p><p>The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot.       <title>Marine life in Gulf of Mexico has still not fully recovered from 2010 BP oil spill</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/22/deepwater-horizon-oil-spill-gulf-marine-life</link>
      <description><p>New study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after Deepwater Horizon disaster</p><p>Marine life in the Gulf of Mexico plummeted by about 60% after BP’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/bp-oil-spill">2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill</a> and has still not fully recovered, according to a new <a href="https://www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.2616554123">study</a>.</p><p>The April 2010<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2014/jun/05/bp-deepwater-horizon-spill-report-failures-risks"> explosion of an offshore drilling </a>unit 50 miles off the Louisiana coast triggered the largest marine oil spill in history, releasing 134m gallons of oil into the ocean. According to the study published on Monday in PNAS, the disaster – which also killed 11 people and injured 17 others – led to the “sudden, severe and persistent declines in the abundance” of marine life for more than a decade.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/22/deepwater-horizon-oil-spill-gulf-marine-life">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>When it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. <![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSat, 24 Oct 2026 11:21:16 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Shares slump slightly as prospects for peace in Middle East seem further away]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/08/11/shares-slump-slightly-as-prospects-for-peace-in-middle-east-seem-further-away/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/08/11/shares-slump-slightly-as-prospects-for-peace-in-middle-east-seem-further-away/Tue, 11 Aug 2026 18:11:13 +0000Global stocks held their nerve on Tuesday, as investors on either side of the Atlantic reacted with differing degrees of confidence that a peace deal will be agreed between the US and Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Closer to home, shares dipped slightly during an otherwise light trading day.

DUBLIN

The Iseq All-Share index fell by 0.32 per cent on Tuesday to close the trading day at 14,233.55, following another light volume session of trading in Ireland.

The banking sector saw mixed results, with AIB’s share price falling by 0.92 per cent to close at €10.76 and PTSB remaining steady on €2.95. Bank of Ireland fared better than its rivals, edging up 0.24 per cent, to end the day at €18.97.

Housebuilder Glenveagh Properties saw its share price rise by 1.62 per cent to close at €2.51, while insulation and building material specialists Kingspan Group was up 1.99 per cent on €97.15 in advance of a €900 million deal that was announced after markets closed.

Stock in wind and solar energy group Greencoat Renewables was up 2.35 per cent, the largest percentage rise of any index constituent.

Glanbia saw its share price fall back 2.41 per cent to close the day at €23.44, while stock in Ryanair also slid, by 0.88 per cent to €24.68.

LONDON

The London Stock Exchange remained largely steady throughout the day. While the blue-chip FTSE 100 index fell by 0.17 per cent, it was somewhat offset by the mid-cap FTSE 250 gaining by 0.22 per cent at close of business.

In a similar day to its Irish neighbours, the UK banking sector saw prices come under pressure. Shares in Lloyds Banking Group on the FTSE 100 fell by 0.74 per cent by close, while NatWest dropped by 0.34 per cent.

Oil and gas giant BP saw much more positive returns, with its shares adding 2.15 per cent despite concerns growing that a peace-deal between the US and Iran, which could reopen the Strait of Hormuz, is looking less likely.

Vodafone Group rebounded by 1.28, having fallen by 3.07 per cent the previous trading day. On the more domestically-focused FTSE 250, shoe makers Doc Marten’s share price rose by 3.34 per cent.

EUROPE

Elsewhere in Europe, stocks remained steady around the record highs they have hovered close to in recent trading days. The pan-European Stoxx 600 rose fractionally, by 0.01 per cent, as investors balanced economic optimism closer to home with geopolitical risks further afield.

With Bloomberg News reporting comments from Pakistan’s defence minister that the US and Iran are nearing “some sort of agreement”, oil prices broadly increased by 1.2 per cent on Tuesday. The energy sector jumped 1.7 per cent, while tech shares rose 1.1 per cent, providing further support. That sector remains among Europe’s top performers this year, up about 24 per cent year to date.

Danish facility manager, ISS gained 4.4 per cent after reporting half-year results above estimates. Spirax Group slid 5.6 per cent to the bottom of the Stoxx 600 after the engineering firm ​reiterated its full-year forecast for mid-single-digit organic revenue growth and margin expansion.

NEW YORK

Early trading of stocks on Wall Street indicated that US investors were matching the caution of their European counterparts, largely avoiding heavy bets on the market.

Both the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell slightly by 1pm New York time, by 0.16 per cent and 0.18 per cent respectively.

The strongest stocks on the S&P during early trade appeared to be investment firm KKR, rising by around 6 per cent, and Axon Enterprise, also around 6 per cent.

Engineering firm Amentum Holdings was in the red from early, with its share price falling some 6 per cent.

Household brand names Apple, Nike and Amazon were off to rocky starts on the Dow Jones Industrial Average Tuesday morning, with the tech giant falling some half a per cent, the sports brand by around 2.6 per cent and the online retail giant by 2.3 per cent. – Additional reporting: Reuters, Bloomberg

]]>Spencer Platt<![CDATA[Mortgage interest rates up slightly but dip below euro zone average]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/08/12/mortgage-interest-rates-up-slightly-but-dip-below-euro-zone-average/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/08/12/mortgage-interest-rates-up-slightly-but-dip-below-euro-zone-average/Wed, 12 Aug 2026 12:39:48 +0000Irish mortgage rates fell below the euro zone average for the first time in over three years in June despite a slight rise in the interest charged on new loans.

The average interest rate on new mortgage agreements at the end of June was 3.49 per cent, according to new Central Bank figures. That is one basis point (0.01 of a percentage point) higher than in May but 11 basis points lower than the same time last year.

That compares with the 0.14 per cent average being offered by the banks for overnight deposits, or 1.86 per cent on fixed term savings.

The average rate of interest on mortgage loans across the euro zone rose faster in the month, to 3.51 per cent, marking the first time the Irish result was lower than the pan-European average since February 2023.

The Irish rate was the 12th highest across the euro bloc in June, according to the Central Bank, falling between the 3.5 per cent average in Italy and the 3.27 per cent in France. Ireland’s position is unchanged from the previous month and down five places from the same time last year.

“Today’s figures confirm what a lot of mortgage holders have been bracing for,” said Sorcha Timoney, mortgage team manager at advisory firm NFP Ireland. “Anyone coming off a fixed rate or on a variable will feel this increase in their monthly repayments.

“Due to strong competition in the Irish market, the gap between what Irish borrowers pay and the wider euro area average has been narrowing but if rates continue to creep up, we could see this gap widening once again,” she said.

The Central Bank data show that fixed rate mortgages accounted for 93 per cent of the volume of all new home loan agreements in June, an increase of eight percentage points from the same period last year. Fixed rate loan interest averaged 3.46 per cent, two basis points higher than in May.

New variable rate mortgages had a weighted average interest rate of 3.96 per cent last month, “the lowest level since December 2022”, the Central Bank said and down seven basis points from May and 12 basis points in annual terms.

Lenders sanctioned €1.1 billion in new mortgage loans in June, up 13 per cent on the May number and the highest figure so far this year. The figure is 8.5 per cent ahead of the €996 million in new loans agreed in the same month last year.

The volume of renegotiated mortgages totalled €586 million last month, €301 million higher than June 2025’s figure and 94 per cent of which had fixed interest rates. People renegotiating their loans did better on interest rates, agreeing an average rate of 3.23 per cent, down two basis points from May and close to a quarter percentage point from this time last year.

Analysts and advisers were quick to point to a number of potential factors for the increase in Irish mortgage interest rates, from competition in the domestic market to ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Trevor Grant, chairman of Irish Mortgage Advisors, said borrowers should not be “unduly alarmed by the widely anticipated September ECB rate hike”, adding that competition was the main factor influencing home loan rates in Ireland.

“Most lenders did not move on the back of the ECB rise in June, though they may see any ECB increase in September as an opportunity to increase rates,” he said.

Rachel McGovern, chief executive of Brokers Ireland, advised people to examine their options.

“Regardless of where you are in the cycle of your loan, now is the time to review because when things turn changes could happen more rapidly than you expect, that is the nature off such changes,” she said, adding that “already we’re seeing niche lenders increasing rates”.

However, as Bonkers.ie spokesman Daragh Cassidy, noted, Ireland’s three big lenders – AIB, Bank of Ireland and PTSB – which account for around 90 per cent of all new mortgage lending in Ireland, have yet to increase their rates.

An analysis by Bonkers.ie found that for an average first-time buyer borrowing €300,000 with a 10 per cent deposit, variable mortgage rates currently range from 3.85 per cent to 4.85 per cent. Rates for a three-year fixed mortgage range from 3.2 per cent to 5.45 per cent, it said.

Away from mortgages, lenders did raise interest rates on other consumer loans more dramatically – by 23 basis points – to 7.48 per cent. The average for variable rates loans – which accounts for over three-quarters of all consumer borrowing – was 8.09 per cent that month, compared to 5.43 per cent for fixed rate loans.

There was €266 million of new consumer borrowing agreed in the month.

On fixed term savings, the 1.86 per cent average available in Ireland is the 13th best rate available across the euro zone, comfortably ahead of the 1.21 per cent in Greece but still well shy of rates above 2.5 per cent available in Finland and the Netherlands.

The Central Bank said Irish savers put €1.6 billion into fixed term deposits in June. That was 14 per cent up on May and 43 per cent stronger than in June 2025.

]]>Andy Rain<![CDATA[Freeze minimum wage until 2030, urges business advisory group]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/14/set-up-350m-ai-training-scheme-and-freeze-minimum-wage-says-business-advisory-group/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/14/set-up-350m-ai-training-scheme-and-freeze-minimum-wage-says-business-advisory-group/Thu, 13 Aug 2026 23:01:00 +0000A €5 billion investment fund, a €350 million artificial intelligence (AI) training programme and no increase in minimum wage until 2030 form part of “a pro-growth agenda” that the Government should adopt to support SMEs, according to a prebudget submission by Azets Ireland.

The professional services firm said that by adopting these measures, and more, the Government would move from “crisis management to strategic investment” for “the next phase of Ireland’s economic success”.

Azets Ireland said small businesses were “the backbone of the domestic economy and employ two in every three workers in local communities across the country” yet were “disproportionately impacted by rising costs and economic uncertainty”.

The advisory company, which employs about 350 people here, called on the Government “to postpone any planned increases in excise duty until greater stability returns to energy markets”, warning that “rising fuel costs could further squeeze already tight margins” for small businesses.

To alleviate these pressures and promote growth in the sector, Azets proposes the creation of a “home-grown investment fund” of €5 billion from “excess corporation tax from multinationals” to be allocated for “strategic investment in small and mid-sized businesses” indigenous to Ireland.

“This fund would help to rebalance the domestic economy and support more firms to grow and compete globally,” the firm said.

It also advocates for “€350 million in funding to be ring-fenced from the National Training Fund for AI skilling and training for SMEs to enable them to upskill their people and enhance future competitiveness”.

“If SMEs are to fully harness the potential of AI, they need greater support to develop the right skills for the future,” Azets Ireland’s chief executive Neil Hughes said.

This “would help businesses build these crucial capabilities and directly enhance future competitiveness”.

It called for “a roadmap to reduce capital gains tax to 20 per cent by 2030, in line with standard rates across Europe”. The standard rate currently applied is 33 per cent.

The firm also advocated for “a simplified route for mid-sized firms to avail of the R&D tax credit”. Hughes said these measures “would help unlock access to much needed capital that can support these businesses accelerate innovation and growth”.

“Amid the escalating cost of doing business, the firm is calling for deferring planned increases in employer PRSI rates to 2027 and a cap on future contribution rates for SMEs,” the company said.

“Azets is also calling for freezing the minimum wage rate until 2030 and additional statutory entitlements for employees to help small and family-owned businesses grappling with rising labour costs.”

Hughes said “with the right supports in place, indigenous businesses can drive the next phase of Irish economic growth, creating jobs, strengthening communities and building a more resilient economy for the future”.

The budget is due to be announced on October 6th by the Minister for Finance Simon Harris and the Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers.

]]>Leah Farrell<![CDATA[Global stocks retreat from record highs amid geopolitical and economic uncertainty]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/13/global-stocks-retreat-from-record-highs-amid-geopolitical-and-economic-uncertainty/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/13/global-stocks-retreat-from-record-highs-amid-geopolitical-and-economic-uncertainty/Thu, 13 Aug 2026 18:00:00 +0000While better-than-expected consumer data in the US boosted investors’ confidence in the market during early trading hours on Wall Street, poor returns for UK-listed mining companies sparked a two-week low on the London Stock Exchange.

DUBLIN

The Iseq All-Share index fell 0.47 per cent on Thursday to close at 14,385.15, following falls in share prices from Ryanair and Great Western Mining.

Building materials group Kingspan saw its share price fall 0.87 per cent on Thursday to close at €102.90.

This comes on the day it announced its acquisition of a majority stake in Grupo Ltd, an Argentinian structural insulated panels manufacturer, and two days after the Cavan-based insulation giant signalled an expansion into its data centre presence with the purchase of BMC Manufacturing Group.

Ryanair’s stock dropped a clean 1 per cent to close on €24.65, while the Nevada-based, Dublin-listed Great Western Mining saw its shares decrease 9.5 per cent, to close on a share price of 3.8 cent.

Kerry Group had a more positive result, with its share price increasing 1.5 per cent to close at €83.90. Glanbia rose 1.20 per cent to €23.64, while Origin Enterprises followed slightly behind, rising 1.01 per cent to close at €4.50.

The banking sector saw mixed returns, with AIB gaining 0.6 per cent to close at €10.69, although Bank of Ireland dropped 0.2 per cent to close at €18.875. Permanent TSB saw no change in its share price, holding at €2.95.

LONDON

The London Stock Exchange was rattled as the blue-chip FTSE 100 index was reduced to a two-week low, a result hardly offset by the more domestically-minded FTSE 250’s increase of 0.1 per cent.

The FTSE 100 fell 0.56 per cent at close after the UK-based Chilean mining company Antofagasta’s downbeat copper production ​forecast sparked losses in the mining sector and offset any relief from stronger-than-expected economic growth in June.

The company’s share fell by 6.8 per cent after it ceased operations at a primary mine. This sparked losses among other mining companies too, with Rio Tinto and Anglo American dropping 4.8 per cent and 3.5 per cent respectively.

Property developer Berkeley saw greater returns, increasing its share price by 2.76 per cent, as did Lion Finance by 5.19 per cent.

EUROPE

Elsewhere in Europe, shares dipped slightly and retreated further from the record highs they reached for days in a row last week, as continental investors grow more cautious about where their money goes.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 index decreased fractionally by 0.04 per cent on Thursday despite impressive gains by some. Dutch payment company Adyen jumped 16.40 at the close of business after it shared financial results from the first half of the year and raised its outlook for the second half.

British companies trading on the euro stock market saw minimal change in their share prices: Lloyds Banking was up 0.09 per cent, oil giant BP was down 1.56 per cent, while Barclays bank decreased 0.08 per cent.

NEW YORK

During early trading hours on Wall Street, US investors felt renewed confidence in the financial markets after better-than-expected producer price data further reduced expectations that the Federal Reserve will increase rates next month.

Both the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 rose before midday New York time, by about 0.2 per cent and 0.7 per cent respectively.

Tech stocks swelled to an intraday record high on the S&P 500 while oil suppliers took a slight hit, with higher inventories and lower global demand forecasts offsetting widespread geopolitical concerns.

Prospects of a US-Iran peace deal were bogged down with renewed pessimism as Washington and Tehran traded accusations that the other party is not prepared to agree to a deal. – Additional reporting: Reuters.

]]>Michael Nagle<![CDATA[NTMA increases State savings rates for first time in three years ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/17/ireland-state-saving-rates-increased-for-first-time-in-three-years/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/17/ireland-state-saving-rates-increased-for-first-time-in-three-years/Mon, 17 Aug 2026 11:27:07 +0000Ireland’s State savings will see an increase in the rates applied to newly-issued products from the end of the month, after the National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) announced its first hike since October 2023.

From August 30th, the variable rate used to calculate the monthly prize bond fund will increase from 1 per cent to 1.5 per cent, meaning “the weekly draw will have more prizes and higher-value prizes,” the NTMA said.

While the monthly top prize of €500,000 will remain unchanged, the weekly top prize will double to €100,000.

Other changes to the fund include 50 prizes of €1,000 being awarded every week, instead of the current arrangement of 20 prizes of €1,000 and 20 of €500. The remaining weekly prizes will increase from €75 to €100.

Some 10,000 prizes are expected to be awarded every week. All prizes are tax free.

The variable rate applied to post-office savings bank deposit accounts will rise by 0.5 per cent to 1.25 per cent, with deposit interest retention tax applied.

The annual equivalent rates (AER) will increase for three-year saving bonds by 0.64 per cent to 1.96 per cent; five-year saving certificate rates by 0.55 per cent to 2.29 per cent; six-year instalment saving rates by 0.58 per cent to 2.33 per cent; and 10-year national solidarity bond rates by 0.65 per cent to 2.66 per cent.

Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris said the move was “a measure that will help people who are saving and investing”.

The various State savings products form part of Ireland’s national debt. The total value of State savings holdings was €23.9 billion at the end June 2026.

The NTMA’s director of funding and debt management, Dave McEvoy, said “retail savings were an important element of the NTMA’s funding strategy, providing diversification in our funding an investor base”.

“In setting rates on Ireland State savings, the NTMA seeks a balance between providing customers with a safe and competitive savings option and providing long-term value to the exchequer,” he said.

]]>Sam boal/Collins Photos<![CDATA[Harvey Nichols Dundrum will not accept gift cards bought before liquidators’ appointment]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/17/harvey-nichols-dundrum-will-not-accept-gift-cards-bought-before-liquidators-appointment/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/17/harvey-nichols-dundrum-will-not-accept-gift-cards-bought-before-liquidators-appointment/Mon, 17 Aug 2026 17:15:53 +0000The provisional liquidators of the Irish company behind the Harvey Nichols store in Dundrum have said they are not currently able to redeem gift cards or fulfil online sales issued by the retailer before they were appointed on August 13th.

John Boland and Nicholas O’Dwyer of Grant Thornton were appointed as joint provisional liquidators last week after the High Court heard the Irish business was insolvent with net liabilities of €28.2 million by the end of the 2026 financial year.

This followed the sale of its UK parent to Mike Ashley’s Frasers group through what is known as a prepack administration process in the UK.

Frasers supplied support for the Dundrum store to reopen on Saturday and to continue trading for now, while the liquidators seek to sell the business.

However, in a notice posted on the Irish store’s website, Harvey Nichols said it was “currently unavailable online” and that any “orders placed and gift cards purchased prior to August 13th, 2026, fall under the ownership structure preceding this transition”.

“Refunds relating to these orders cannot be processed by Harvey Nichols directly; customers with an outstanding refund from this period are asked to contact, HNCustomers@fticonsulting.com.”

In a statement to The Irish Times in relation to gift cards and online orders, the liquidators said they had “entered into an arrangement” that enabled the Dundrum store to open again for trading from August 15th.

“The arrangement allows the business to continue trading and receive stock while the JPLs [joint provisional liquidators] assess the options available to the company,” they added.

Harvey Nichols Dundrum was kept on life support for 20 years. But could it still have a future?

“Continued trading helps preserve value in the business, maintain employment and provides an opportunity to determine whether a sale or other transaction can be achieved in the interests of the company stakeholders. At this time, there can be no certainty as to the outcome of that process.

The liquidators said they were “continuing to assess the position in relation to gift cards and advise that they cannot currently be accepted in store”.

“Customers who hold gift cards are advised to retain them while that review is ongoing. A further update will be provided once the position has been determined. The situation regarding online orders is also still under review.”

In its statement to the London Stock Exchange last week on the Harvey Nichols deal, Frasers said “certain assets located at the Dublin store including stock and store fixtures have been acquired as part of the transaction. Discussions in relation to the business are ongoing and Frasers continues to support the trading operations of the Dublin store.”

The Dundrum store was closed last Friday but reopened on Saturday. It has 33 staff and pays annual rent of just more than €1 million for the Dundrum outlet, which first opened in 2005.

One employee working at the outlet on Monday told The Irish Times that although staff “did know the store was up for sale”, learning that it was deemed insolvent and unable to pay its debts “was a surprise”.

There appeared to be an equal number of staff and customers in the store around lunchtime on Monday.

“It’s very sad,” one shopper said, wondering about the future employment of the workers inside. “But the issue is there’s never anyone in there,” she said. “I hardly ever come here to use it […] it’s so off the beaten track.”

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Global stocks falter amid Middle East conflict and looming economic data]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/17/global-stokes-falter-amid-middle-east-conflict-and-looming-economic-data/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/08/17/global-stokes-falter-amid-middle-east-conflict-and-looming-economic-data/Mon, 17 Aug 2026 17:11:20 +0000Global stocks largely faltered on Monday – in the US, peace in the Middle East seems further away and continues to trouble investors’ confidence. Meanwhile in the United Kingdom, looming employment and inflation data led many investors to hold their bets.

Dublin

]]>Colin Keegan<![CDATA[Irish business leaders on the move: 10 key leadership changes in 2025 and 2026]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/24/irish-business-leaders-on-the-move-10-key-leadership-changes-in-2025-and-2026/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/24/irish-business-leaders-on-the-move-10-key-leadership-changes-in-2025-and-2026/Thu, 24 Sep 2026 09:00:00 +0000Corporate Ireland has felt its fair share of movement at board level over the past year, from the appointment of a managing director tasked with the overhaul of national operations to the disputed ousting of a chairman.

Here, The Irish Times profiles 10 of the most notable recent moves in Irish business.

Marian Finnegan

After nearly 30 years of working for the country’s largest real estate agency, Marian Finnegan’s service to Sherry Fitzgerald led to her taking up the group’s chief executive role in September last year.

She is the first woman at the helm of the company, which employs 360 people in over 100 offices. Within six months of Finnegan’s promotion to the top job, the firm specialising in residential properties acquired its rival Knight Frank, which focuses on commercial properties.

In an interview with The Irish Times, Finnegan said she saw a “tiny” job advertisement on the back page of this newspaper for an economist position at the firm in 1996. After 29 years, while managing director of the residential arm of the company, Finnegan said “it felt like the natural next step” to head the business.

The top position had been left vacant since February 2025 following the exit of Steven McKenna, who has since founded his own advisory firm.

Kenny Jacobs

In February of this year, the High Court heard Kenny Jacobs would “voluntarily step down” as chief executive of the DAA, which operates Dublin and Cork airports, after an out-of-court settlement closed the lawsuit brought against the semi-State body.

Suspended from his position just before Christmas following a months-long rift with DAA colleagues, Jacobs had previously agreed an exit package with its board, however Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien refused to sign off on it.

Following an ugly court case – what is seen as the fieriest feud to engulf the airport operator in decades – Jacobs ultimately left with a parting sum in the region of €480,000.

In July, the Cork-born businessman was appointed chairman and president of Manna, the drone delivery service that paused operations in Ireland the previous month and is now focusing on the US and UK markets.

Garry Moroney

Marking a departure from the managing director title bestowed on previous commercial leaders of The Irish Times Group, tech-exec-turned-media-mogul Garry Moroney was appointed its first chief executive in November 2025.

He took over in January 2026 from the interim chief executive Michael Sheehan, who reverted to his previous position of chief financial officer. Previously chief executive of travel management platform Roomex, Moroney had founded two companies before this and worked at McKinsey at the start of his career.

Alongside this newspaper, the group owns the Irish Examiner and Echo, a range of regional newspapers and websites MyHome.ie and RIP.ie. In early August, it announced its intention to wind down breakingnews.ie.

Deirdre Veldon, the former deputy editor of The Irish Times, stepped down as the group’s managing director in September 2025 having served in the position since late 2022.

Andrew Yaxley

UK-based Tesco Group reshuffled its Irish operations in August, with former Tesco Ireland chief executive Andrew Yaxley returning to lead the all-island business here after eight years in Britain.

He effectively traded roles with Geoff Byrne, who will take over as chief executive of the wholesaler Booker Group in September. Both men will continue to sit on the group’s executive committee.

Yaxley, who has worked for the supermarket giant for over 25 years in Ireland, Britain and Czech Republic, had been head of the Irish arm of the retailer from 2015 to 2018.

He was promoted by then-Tesco chief, now-Diageo chief, Dave Lewis, to the chief product officer role in the supermarket group, amid a major restructuring push.

Conor Neiland

Perhaps another beneficiary of Dave Lewis’s inclination to overhaul operations, Conor Neiland took over the role of managing director of Diageo Ireland in July.

The University of Galway graduate has worked for the drinks giant – which owns Guinness, Bewleys, Smirnoff vodka and Johnnie Walker whiskey – for 21 years, with managing director stints in the Seychelles islands, South Korea and Colombia.

Not long after his appointment, the UK-based parent company announced its intention to save £1 billion (€866 million) over the next three years through supply chain reform and job cuts.

It is understood some 150 jobs are at risk within the group’s 1,200 person-strong workforce in Ireland. Louise Ryan left the managing director role in June, after one year in the post.

Caroline Bocquel

Moving from the top job at Ireland’s Seafood Development Agency (Bord Iascaigh Mhara) to the top job at the State’s national tourism development authority, Caroline Bocquel was appointed chief executive of Fáilte Ireland in November last year.

The first woman to lead the State agency, she previously chaired the audit and risk committee in the Environmental Protection Agency and, before that, served as chief financial officer of the global charity Goal.

Fáilte Ireland’s previous chief executive, Paul Kelly, left the tourism authority in March after eight years in the post. He now serves as chief executive of the Royal Dublin Society (RDS).

Albert Manifold

In an unexpected move that attracted international headlines, Templeogue-born Albert Manifold was ousted as chairman of British oil and gas giant BP with immediate effect in late May.

The company said “serious concerns” were raised with relation to “important governance standards, oversight and conduct”. Manifold said he was removed “without warning and without explanation” and rejected “lies” spread about his personal and professional conduct.

Shares in BP dropped 4 per cent on the London Stock Exchange the day Manifold was removed, as many investors questioned the stability of the company. The same day, Ian Tyler was appointed as BP’s interim chair.

Eoin Tonge

Primark returned to its Irish leadership roots with the appointment of Eoin Tonge as its chief executive in March this year, 17 years after its founder Arthur Ryan left the position.

Between the two, from 2009 to 2025, the role was held by British-born Paul Marchant, who resigned in March last year following an investigation into alleged inappropriate behaviour towards a female colleague.

Tonge had acted as interim chief executive from the conclusion of the investigation but was announced as a permanent successor a year later.

The retailer’s parent company, Associated British Foods, is moving forward with plans to demerge the fashion giant from grocery businesses under its portfolio by late 2027.

Fergal Leamy

With the exit of David McRedmond after a decade as the head of An Post in August, the chief executive title is to pass next to Fergal Leamy, the former head of Coillte, the State-owned forestry company and Glen Dimplex, a privately-owned manufacturing and heating group.

As the then executive director of Transport for West Midlands – “one of the biggest transport authorities in the UK” – she was tasked with a transport strategy for the 2022 Commonwealth Games held in Birmingham.

She now oversees the long-awaited Dublin MetroLink and a Dart-like service in Cork city. Upon her appointment, Shaw said she was “excited to begin work to continue the journey of improving transport for the people of Ireland”.

Representing himself before the WRC earlier this month, Hayes said he started his career as a trainee at the Department of Posts and Telegraphs in October 1980, prior to Eircom being founded with the privatisation of the telecoms system.

His evidence was that he attended a medical appointment with an occupational health assessor in June 2024 and was deemed “fit for work”.

Hayes added that after his retirement on September 24th, 2024, he was brought on by a third-party contractor to do work for Eircom which was “identical” to what he was doing before.

In February 2025, Peter Woods paid €2.5 million for Nirvana on Coliemore Road, Dalkey.

Woods has lodged plans with Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council to demolish Nirvana and construct three new houses on the site.

The houses would comprise a 349sq m three-storey, four-bedroom dwelling with a sauna; and two two-storey, three-bedroom dwellings of 124sq m each.

A report by planning consultant Kiaran O’Malley, concerning the Woods application, said that, initially, Woods had intended to renovate Nirvana “but following a number of radon surveys and remediation measures, the radon levels could not be brought down to safe levels so it was recommended to demolish the house”.

Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas and is classified as a group-one carcinogen and is the second-biggest cause of lung cancer in Ireland.

Radon is colourless, odourless and tasteless and can be measured only using specialised equipment.

Tests carried out at Nirvana by Cora Consulting Engineers between May and July 2025 detected radon levels more than five times the maximum limit for a domestic house and 13 times the average level in Ireland.
