]]> As Ukraine continues to defend itself against Russia’s invasion, European startups are developing technologies ranging from autonomous drones and air-defence systems to satellite intelligence, with venture capital playing an increasingly important role in supporting defence innovation.

EU-Startups’ reporting on European DefenceTech and adjacent dual-use technologies has identified more than €1.8 billion in financing across 22 European startups in 2026, as of October.

Drawing on EU-Startups’ coverage, we’ve put together a list of European startups that secured funding in 2026 and are contributing to Ukraine’s defence efforts, alongside the investors backing them. Together, this list represents over €1 billion of funds raised for direct intervention in Ukraine.

And stay tuned: we have an upcoming EU-Startups Podcast episode featuring one of the startups on this list!

The Defenders

DOD Solution – Estonia/Ukraine: Founded in 2023, DOD Solution is an Estonian-Ukrainian DefenceTech startup developing AI-powered autonomy for unmanned systems. Its AURA AI platform combines onboard computing and software to provide autonomous navigation, target recognition and tracking, even when GPS signals or communications are unavailable. Unlike technologies still awaiting frontline validation, AURA AI has already been used in combat in Ukraine.

In September 2026, the company raised €1.8 million in pre-Seed funding from Angel One Fund, Better Angle, Defence Builder Fund, Network VC, Newfund, UAID Fund, WildField Ventures and 4C-Next Holding AG, alongside strategic investor Draganfly. The financing will support product development and further integrations with Ukrainian drone manufacturers.

Frankenburg Technologies – Estonia: Founded in 2024 and headquartered in Tallinn, Frankenburg Technologies develops affordable, mass-manufacturable missile defence systems intended to counter drones and other aerial threats. Co-founded by Taavi Madiberk and Marko Virkebau, the startup is developing its Mark I short-range interceptor missile, with an emphasis on reducing production costs and increasing manufacturing capacity. Its operations extend across eight countries, including Ukraine, reflecting its ambition to manufacture defensive systems closer to where they are needed.

In February 2026, Frankenburg secured €30 million in Series A funding led by Plural, with participation from SmartCap, bringing its reported total funding to €40 million.

ICEYE – Finland: Founded in 2014 and headquartered in Espoo, ICEYE develops and operates synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites capable of capturing high-resolution imagery regardless of weather conditions or daylight. Its technology supports defence intelligence and battlefield monitoring, including for Ukraine’s armed forces, which benefit from satellite imagery to improve situational awareness.

In January 2026, ICEYE expanded its cooperation with Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to provide additional space-based intelligence. In June, the company announced a €450 million primary Series F investment led by General Atlantic, with investors including Solidium, Tesi, Varma, Ilmarinen, Lifeline Ventures, Nokia, QIA and TCV. The Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, was subsequently identified as a co-lead. Including secondary transactions, the financing exceeded €1 billion.

Occam Industries – United Kingdom: Founded in 2025 and based in London, Occam Industries develops autonomous drone technology designed to reduce reliance on human pilots in battlefield conditions. Its OccamX platform uses computer vision to enable FPV drones to navigate and track targets without continuous manual control or GPS connectivity. Occam has also completed initial testing through Ukraine’s Brave1 defence innovation cluster, opening the door to integration trials with Ukrainian drone manufacturers and potential deployment with the country’s armed forces.

In February 2026, the startup raised €3 million in pre-Seed funding led by Presto Tech Horizons, with participation from Antler, Freedom Fund, TYR.vc and defence-sector angel investors.

PDKINEMATICS – Lithuania: Founded in 2025 and headquartered in Vilnius, PDKINEMATICS develops precision-guidance systems for unmanned aerial vehicles, helping drones operate more accurately in environments affected by electronic warfare. Its flagship Gannet technology enables UAVs to release munitions from higher altitudes without sacrificing accuracy. The startup has partnered with Ukrainian drone manufacturer Bavovna.ai, integrating its systems into platforms already deployed in battlefield conditions.

In June 2026, PDKINEMATICS secured €2 million in Seed funding co-led by Coinvest Capital and Iron Wolf Capital, bringing its total funding to €3 million. The investment will support increased manufacturing capacity and further deployments across Ukraine and European defence markets.

Quantum Systems – Germany: Founded in 2015 and based near Munich, Quantum Systems develops AI-powered unmanned aerial systems and software for military reconnaissance and autonomous operations. The company has an established presence in Ukraine, where its drones reportedly completed more than 19,000 missions during 2025.

In July 2026, it announced a €1 billion Series D round co-led by Blackstone, Noteus, Airbus and Advent, with backing from BOND, Fidelity, Wellington Management, A.P. Moller Holding, Elephant Lake Ventures, Balderton and HV Capital. Its Ukrainian operations are also expanding: in October 2026, EU-Startups reported plans for tens of thousands of Germany-funded interceptor drones to be manufactured in Ukraine.

Shotling – Denmark: Danish DefenceTech startup Shotling develops short-range counter-drone systems designed to protect military personnel, vehicles and infrastructure against FPV drones and loitering munitions. Its electrically driven rotary shotgun system uses a high-capacity magazine and is designed for integration into mobile or stationary defence platforms. The technology addresses a challenge encountered by Ukrainian forces: intercepting inexpensive attack drones without relying on disproportionately costly defensive systems.

In February 2026, Shotling announced €700k in pre-Seed financing led by Myriad Defense Fund, with participation from IPO CLUB’s Fund II America 2030 and a non-dilutive match-loan from EIFO. The startup has reportedly received support from Ukrainian frontline units and defence companies, although operational deployment details have not been disclosed.

Special Mention

Varangians – Sweden: Beyond the startups developing defence technologies, Stockholm-based Varangians represents a more direct route for European venture capital into Ukraine’s DefenceTech ecosystem. Co-founded by Pär Lager, Andreas Flodström and Jonas Rydin alongside a Swedish family office, the investment fund announced a close of more than €10 million in June 2026, specifically to support Ukrainian defence innovation.

Its portfolio includes Norda Dynamics, which develops autonomous drone piloting technology for communications-denied environments; Himera, specialising in electronic-warfare-resistant secure communications; and Sine Engineering, which builds UAV communication and positioning systems capable of operating under jamming and interference.

]]> Cognitive Credit, the London-based provider of corporate credit data, analytics and AI technology, has secured a €35.73 million ($40 million) strategic growth investment.

The investment round was led by global growth equity firm Summit Partners, with continued participation from existing investor ETFS Capital. The investment follows an €8.93 million ($10 million) Series B led by ETFS Capital in September 2024, and a €7.17 million (£6 million) Series A led by Fitch Ventures in November 2021

“High-quality data at speed and scale is critical to powering AI workflows that credit professionals will increasingly rely on for high-stakes decisions,” said Chris Bon, a Partner at Summit Partners who has joined the Cognitive Credit Board of Directors.

Founded in 2017 by Robert Slater, Cognitive Credit was built by ex-credit analysts who experienced first-hand the limitations of relying on tools designed for equity markets, at a time when no credible alternative existed for the credit space. The company set out to address what it saw as a long-overdue digital transformation in corporate credit markets, one of the world’s largest asset classes with nearly €12.5 trillion ($14 trillion) raised in 2025 alone, according to OECD’s Global Debt Report 2026.

Cognitive Credit’s integrated web application provides support across the credit research workflow, combining verified data, advanced analytics and domain-specialist generative AI capabilities. Its platform is powered by proprietary data developed through the analysis of hundreds of thousands of financial reports to give analysts on-demand access to audit-grade credit models and primary reporting libraries across 3,500+ corporate bond and loan issuers in the US, Europe and emerging markets.

“Cognitive Credit is purpose-built for credit analysis and leverages institutional-grade technology to provide speed, precision, and auditability across thousands of issuers and to support leading banks and asset managers in use cases where accuracy and verifiability are critical. We’re excited to partner with Robert and the team as they further expand their presence and offering and help credit professionals put AI to work with confidence,” added Bon.

Cognitive Credit’s product suite includes a web application, an Excel add-in that streams proprietary financials directly into existing spreadsheets, a REST API for integration into institutional tech stacks, and a Claude Connector that allows analysts to query issuers and surface financial insights directly from within the Claude environment.

The company says all the outputs are fully auditable and traceable to source, a critical differentiator for institutional clients. This emphasis on verified data could be the reason why the company has managed to power analytical workflows for more than 80% of the top 25 global asset managers by AUM and all top 10 global debt league table investment banks. In a statement, Summit Partners says Cognitive Credit has achieved 240% active user growth and more than doubled its global bond and loan issuer coverage.

“Demand for credit-specialist technology will continue to accelerate from here, and we are pleased to partner with Summit Partners on our next phase of growth. With the imminent launch of DealConnect, ongoing innovation in our AI deployments, and many additional capabilities planned for 2027, we’re offering credit teams the highest quality data and analytics they require for differentiated analysis and high impact decision-making,” said Slater, founder and CEO of Cognitive Credit.

With this strategic investment, Cognitive Credit will accelerate its commercial expansion into the US and advance its next generation of products. These include the imminent launch of DealConnect, designed to enable on-demand access to detailed credit models for private issuers that report via secure data rooms, and the pending deployment of agentic credit analysis. The company also plans to continue expanding its issuer coverage into new credit markets.

The post OPINION: Robotics are essential for Europe’s energy transition appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Europe’s energy transition story is usually told through assets: more renewable generation, smarter grids, electric vehicles and battery storage. Yet while much of the debate focuses on financing and building infrastructure, a different challenge is emerging beneath the surface: operating and maintaining a rapidly expanding asset base over the next several decades.

But the high-margin subsidised programmes that kick-started the industry are being phased out, and operators are facing a new reality of low-margin operations at scale. Combined with the demographic squeeze on the European workforce, the industry looks ripe for automation. Maybe even for robots.

The problem is well-known and systemic. Transmission networks are aging – some 40% of Europe’s distribution grids are over 40 years old – and cross-border capacity is set to double. Offshore wind is moving further from shore and into deeper water. Solar is multiplying faster than construction and maintenance teams can keep up with.

The jobs required to operate all of this are highly skilled or physically demanding and impossible to scale quickly: rope-access technicians, electrical engineers, subsea specialists, offshore crews. You cannot train a generation of them in a hiring cycle, and Europe’s demographics make the recruitment harder every year.

On the other side sits the newest trend in AI. “Physical AI” – large models and computer vision wrapped around a machine that moves – feeds hope for something close to a science-fiction solution. Capital has followed: foundation models for robotics, task-specific platforms, middleware to run fleets. What was research five years ago is now in early production across several industries, also by European energy operators. Among European energy operators, though, the pilot is still the standard unit of deployment.

Reality moves slower, but the underlying idea – raise output and de-risk demographics at the same time – is understood, and it does not require full autonomy to pay off. For now it is about making the people already on the payroll more productive: engineers delivering higher inspecting output, system designs that remove the need to send a crew into a hostile environment, machines that facilitate maintenance work with little manual additions. These advancements create capacity without waiting years for new workers. The infrastructure can keep scaling even when headcount cannot.

The build is financed but the operating cost is the open question

Europe is entering a period of extraordinary expansion. Solar capacity needs to grow 107% by 2030, wind 84%, electricity demand 60%, and transmission must roughly triple – with nearly €600 billion of grid investment needed between now and the end of the decade. In practical terms that means around 150 million solar panels and 150,000 wind turbines to install and then keep running, alongside an existing asset base that is getting older.

For most of the last two decades this was very lucrative, derisked through subsidised feed-in tariffs over up to 20 years. As feed-in tariffs phase out and CfDs roll in and new builds compete at market prices, operating on thin margins becomes normality.

The hardware got cheap, the margin moved

For years robotics was simply too expensive for this work. That has inverted, though not quite in the way the headlines suggest.

LiDAR is projected to fall from around €4,297 ($5,000) to €1,203 ($1,400) by 2040, actuators have roughly halved, battery packs sit near €92.81/kWh ($108/kWh), and inference at the edge costs cents per hour.

Autonomy has matured alongside it: transformer-based approaches have cut the demonstrations needed to teach a new task from tens of thousands to a few dozen, and most of the training now happens in simulation before anything is flown or driven near a live substation.

None of this favours European hardware manufacturers directly. Chinese robot makers undercut European prices by 20 to 30%, and in some cases by up to 50%. For investors, the profits need to be made on the intelligence. Two software layers decide whether a fleet of cheap sensors and commodity actuators actually becomes useful to an energy operator, rather than an expensive way to generate footage nobody watches.

The first is physical observability: the ability to reliably capture, attribute and continuously refresh real-world asset conditions. A thermal camera, microphone or LiDAR scanner only creates value when the observation can be tied to a specific transformer, switchgear compartment or span, stored in context, and compared against its operating history.

The challenge is therefore not simply collecting more data, but capturing the right signals at the right frequency and linking them to the correct asset. In critical infrastructure, where access is difficult, hazards are high and failure modes are rare, this observability layer becomes the prerequisite for any meaningful intelligence.

The second is spatial interpretation: turning what a camera sees into something an energy operator can act on. A generic vision model can flag discolouration on a turbine blade; a system built for energy assets can place that defect on the span, compare its progression against the rest of the fleet, check it against the threshold that triggers a mandatory inspection, and decide whether it justifies pulling a technician forward or waiting for the next weather window.

That judgement comes from fusing thermal, visual and historical inspection data against a specific asset class, and from having seen enough of those assets to know what normal looks like. Together, they form a loop that gets more valuable with every site added, because the data behind it cannot be bought off a shelf.

Why now is the time to act

Two regulatory dates give this some urgency. The EU Machinery Regulation applies from 20 January 2027, and it treats AI safety components as high-risk, requiring certification through a notified body. The AI Act’s obligations for robots operating in critical infrastructure follow on 2nd August 2028, covering transparency, technical documentation and post-market monitoring. Companies that can show compliance evidence alongside their product will move faster through procurement than those retrofitting it under deadline pressure.

Components will likely keep coming from Asia, and much of the underlying AI research from the US. Both enable value creation within Europe. The layer that captures the profits orchestrates customer needs, European and national regulation, and earns the operator’s trust through tangible results. That is where Europe is genuinely positioned to win, provided founders and investors resist the temptation to compete where the economics do not favour them.

]]> Cygrid, a Berlin-based cybersecurity startup, has exited stealth with a €2.66 million pre-Seed funding round for its identity-enforcement platform that controls access to confidential information. 

The funding round was led by Atlantic, the pan-European pre-Seed fund, with participation from D11Z. Ventures, alongside angel investors including Boris Gorin, VP Product at Zscaler and founder of Canonic Security; Andreas Bermig, CEO of bonify; and Vlad Tropko of AmberVale Capital.

“Dmitry and Dekel are proven builders who combine deep cybersecurity experience with a real understanding of what enterprises need: security that stops the wrong action without slowing the business down. AI agents are widening the identity attack surface faster than any control can keep up. Intelligence-driven enforcement is the only answer that scales. The timing for Cygrid couldn’t be better,” said Marc-Olivier Lücke, General Partner, Atlantic.

Cygrid was founded in January 2026 by Dmitry Kharchenko and Dekel Paz, both of whom served in the Israeli Military Intelligence. The pair identified a security blind spot created by the rapid proliferation of AI agents inside enterprises, and Cygrid solves this by changing how identity and access management works at the enterprise level.

Unlike conventional identity and access management tools, which grant access at sign-in and stop there, Cygrid enforces limits continuously, checking each action an agent takes and blocking or narrowing it in real time. It also maps human, non-human and AI agent identities into a single intelligence graph, correlating what each identity is entitled to, what it actually does, and on whose behalf it acts. The company argues this approach lets it revoke a forgotten token in seconds and stop a risky AI agent command before it executes.

“Access control tells you who can log in. It says nothing about what they do next. Every identity in an enterprise can act, and once a token is valid, not one control in the stack can stop the action. Cygrid is the platform that does: it decides what each identity may do and enforces it before anything executes,” said Kharchenko, CEO and co-founder, Cygrid.

In just nine months after incorporation, Cygrid is already serving 19 design partners across FinTech, e-commerce, and SaaS verticals, with six in production. In one early deployment, a Berlin-based D2C company discovered AI agents and third-party app connections its own security team was unaware of, and used Cygrid to remediate more than 100 risky findings.

The fundraise follows a rise in attacks on trusted identities. According to Palo Alto Networks, machine identities now outnumber human ones by 109 to 1, with 79 of those being AI agents. A CrowdStrike report from 2026 found that 82% of cyber detections involve no malware whatsoever; the attackers simply exploited trusted identities such as leaked tokens or compromised agent providers.

With more than 80% of Fortune 500 companies already deploying AI agents and nearly a third of employees using connected agents without organisational approval, according to Microsoft’s Cyber Pulse report 2026, Cygrid sees an urgent, wide-open opportunity.

The startup will use the fresh capital toward expanding its enforcement capabilities, growing its team, and scaling go-to-market operations across Europe. It aims to become the European alternative to US and Israeli providers of AI identity security.

“This funding allows us to scale that approach and help organisations move from reactive identity security to continuous, real-time enforcement, so they can adopt AI agents at full speed without losing control of what those agents can do,” added Kharchenko.

]]> Intuitivo, a Portuguese EdTech startup that helps lighten teachers’ administrative load, has raised €1.35 million in Seed funding.

The round was led by Caixa Capital and the Impact Innovation Fund, managed by 3xP Global under the Venture Capital Programme of the Capitalisation and Resilience Fund (FdCR), administered by Banco Português de Fomento, Portugal’s development bank. Global accelerator Techstars, COREangels Lisboa and COREangels Porto also took part, alongside Angels Way, the first Portuguese fund structured as a community, pooling together 436 small investors.

“Intuitivo was born from a teacherʼs request and continues to be developed together with teachers. Our goal is simple: to give time back to those who teach,” said João Guimarães, co-founder and CEO of Intuitivo.

Founded in 2021 by Guimarães, Duarte Oliveira and Diogo Silva, Intuitive is a digital assessment platform designed to enable educators to create, schedule and grade tests and deliver feedback to students. It covers everything from primary school to higher education.

Teachers on the platform can build assessments from scratch, draw from a shared exercise library, or use AI to convert old PDF tests into fully interactive, auto-graded digital versions. Students, on the other hand, access their tests through a single link, no need for an account or software installation.

The platform also gives teachers real-time monitoring during live assessments, built-in anti-cheating mechanisms, and automatic performance statistics broken down by student, class and exercise. Intuitive is solving a well-documented problem ,with OECD’s TALIS 2024 survey revealing that actual teaching accounts for just 43% of a teacher’s working time, with Portugal ranking first among the 44 countries studied in time spent on assessment and grading.

Intuitivo estimates it helps teachers save around 165,000 hours of working time in the 2025/26 school year alone. The startup counts 75,000 registered teachers among its users and has secured more than 200 contracts with municipalities, school clusters and private schools, covering more than 500 schools across Portugal.

While it frees up teachers from administrative tasks, school leadership also benefits from its centralised dashboard to track results and teacher adoption across an entire institution.

The fresh funding will be used to deepen product development and nearly double its headcount from 11 to 20 employees before the end of this year. The startup also plans to use the funding to expand beyond Portugal and break into Brazil, a market estimated at 2.2 million teachers, roughly twelve times the size of its home market.

“Brazil is the natural step: it speaks our language, has more than 2 million teachers, teachers there adopt digital tools easily, and some already use Intuitivo. We want to take what we have built in Portugal there, on a much bigger scale,” added Guimarães.

]]> The CLARITY Act was designed to set clearer rules for how digital assets are classified and overseen in the US. Its failure in the Senate leaves American investors without that framework for now, and anyone watching the Ethereum price USD chart saw the reaction within hours.

The much-lauded CLARITY Act failed to advance in the US Senate on Tuesday, September 15, in a severe setback for the digital assets and crypto industry. It fell 11 votes short of the 60-vote threshold it needed to move onward in the 100-seat chamber. Primarily put forward by Republican lawmakers, three of them voted against it, joining every Senate Democrat in opposition, and the motion failed. The impact will be felt by anyone who trades digital assets, in the US and abroad.

How did markets respond to the Clarity Act failure?

Markets responded quickly to the news. Binance market data showed Bitcoin dropping 5% after the vote. At the time of writing (September 18), it had rebounded slightly, climbing to $78,180 from a $75,390 low on Tuesday, September 15. Ether stood at $2,515, up from $2,378 the day after the vote. Share prices of several crypto firms also fell, with Coinbase and Circle each down about 10%, according to Cointelegraph.

This will push any further decisions on it until after the mid-term elections, which will take place in November. A key fight to take control of the House and Senate, it could potentially be pushed back until 2029 should Democrats make it a priority and stop it dead in its tracks.

What was the Clarity Act?

The CLARITY Act was an attempt to provide a US federal framework for digital asset markets. For years, there has been confusion over where digital assets lie in the US and who has oversight for them. Primarily, this was the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

Where value is derived from network use and trading, in spot markets, jurisdiction would have been given to the CFTC. The SEC would have had an overview of digital securities in which the value depended on a specific company’s managerial efforts.

How have banks reacted to the Clarity Act news?

The US Banking lobby has already pledged its support to keep fighting for the bill. This is mainly because it still leaves questions around stablecoin yields unanswered. A joint statement from the Independent Community Bankers of America and American Bankers Association noted that “as lawmakers consider next steps, we encourage them to adopt targeted changes to stablecoin yield policy.”

It is likely this will now pivot the conversation to how banks can begin to implement the GENIUS Act. Signed into law in 2025, it has barred stablecoin issuers from offering rewards. Yet it does allow third parties, such as exchanges, to pay yields. The Independent Community Bankers of America has warned that this could drain as much as $1.3 trillion from community bank deposits.

Stablecoin builders outside the US are watching this fight closely: EU-Startups reported in July 2025 that London fintech Due had raised €6.3 million and launched a stablecoin API for borderless payments, the kind of product whose US reach depends on how Washington settles yield.

How did crypto exchanges react?

The major crypto exchanges were keen to point out that by no means does this signal the end for the CLARITY Act. Binance added that “With the November midterm elections approaching, lawmakers have limited time to resolve disagreements and secure the votes needed to move the bill forward. A renewed attempt would still have to navigate Senate procedures and any remaining legislative steps, including resolving differences with the House-passed version before legislation could reach the president.” They then closed this with “The immediate result is a stalled bill, not necessarily a permanently dead one.”

Other crypto companies also released statements on the event. Ripple described this as a “tremendous missed opportunity” in a statement on their website. They went on to add that “Consumers and market participants still deserve predictable standards and protections. Responsible businesses should not have to rely on years of litigation or live under the threat of one to understand how the law applies to them. And the United States should not concede leadership in the future of finance because policymakers were unable to establish a durable framework. Ripple will continue advocating for market structure legislation and engaging constructively with policymakers.”

This will only add to the volatility the crypto market has displayed over the last few months. Rising oil prices and expectations that the Federal Reserve would hike rates, which it did on Wednesday, September 16, have also weighed on sentiment.

Further dampening the mood were comments signaling that investors should not write off the prospect of another rate raise before the year is out. This was the first rate rise in three years, taking them to 3.75%-4%, according to the Federal Reserve’s September 16 statement, as reported by CNBC. After the September 16 decision, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long“, then branded the move a “sober” and “responsible decision“. He then highlighted that inflation remains a problem, showing that more may yet be due to come.

]]> In May 2026, hopes of a British-designed successor to the RAF‘s Hawk fleet faded when aerospace start-up Aeralis collapsed.

With no domestic contender remaining, the replacement for the RAF’s Hawk T1 and Hawk T2 aircraft is now likely to be based on an overseas design.

The Hawk has been one of Britain’s most successful military aircraft programmes and export successes.

However, with the Hawk T1 due to retire from RAF service around 2030 and the wider Hawk fleet approaching the end of its operational life, a replacement will need to be selected in the near future.

The programme to find a Hawk replacement

In 2026, the UK Ministry of Defence issued a request for information to replace its Hawk aircraft. It requires a new trainer for its Red Arrows to serve as an aerobatic aircraft and a replacement for its 28 (now 27) Hawk T2 trainers.

The MoD is likely to select a common platform for the two aircraft variants, so whichever design wins the T1 competition will likely also be the one winning the T2 competition.

The MoD has said the aircraft should be “designed to support the transition to fifth- and sixth-generation air systems, ensuring UK pilots are equipped with the skills needed for modern and future combat environments.”

Prospective contractors were to place their submissions by the 11 September. A key requirement was for Britain to have a significant workshare.

BAE-Boeing-Saab T-7 Red Hawk

BAE Systems has announced a partnership with Boeing to offer the T-7 Red Hawk (designed for the US Air Force) to the Royal Air Force. This is widely viewed asthe most likely option for the Hawk T1 and T2 replacement.

BAE stated in July, “The agreement marks a significant milestone in the partnership between the three companies and commits to a new UK-based final assembly and integration facility.”

The T7 is undergoing flight testing, is set to enter serial production, and is soon to enter service with the US Air Force. The type would be a comparatively low-risk option and an aircraft that has been designed for future improvements.

BAE CEO ​Charles Woodburn said, “Our offer represents a modern, integrated training solution which aligns with the ambition of the Defence Investment Plan, while ​strengthening the UK’s sovereign industrial capability.”

Italy’s Leonardo M-346 Master

The Leonardo M-346 Master is a popular and capable trainer that has the benefit of being a mature aircraft and would help the UK build on its close relationship with Italy.

The Master is regarded as one of the leading alternatives to the T-7.

The Italian Air Force selected the M-346 for its national aerobatic team, the Frecce Tricolori, in 2024. These will replace the team’s existing fleet of ten Aermacchi MB-339s. The team will receive the first in 2027 and transition in 2028.

Overall, the Leonardo M-346 offers lower development risk as the T-7 is not yet mature. It is also already in service with the air forces of Italy, Israel, Poland, Singapore, Qatar, and Greece.

The contracting British party is Babcock.

Other, less likely, options

The other two bidding aircraft are the Lockheed Martin KAI TF-50 and the Turkish Aerospace Hürjet. These are generally considered by industry experts as being less likely to win, especially the Hürjet.

Lockheed and South Korea’s KAI are offering a version of the popular T-50 Golden Eagle family. The aircraft first entered service in 2005, and variants have since been exported to Poland, Indonesia, Iraq, the Philippines, and Thailand.

Like the M-348, the Golden Eagle is also a mature design offering low risk. Notably, since 2010, South Korea’s Black Eagles aerobatic display team has also used the T-50B Golden Eagle as its display aircraft.

Turkey is also offering the Hürjet single-engine advanced trainer, which it is delivering as an advanced trainer, aerobatic display aircraft, and for light-combat missions.

Its unclear if the jet would realistically be ready within the RAF’s 2030 timeframe.

In 2025, Spain approved a budget of around $3.6 billion to purchase up to 45 upcoming Hürjet jets, showing there is some solid export interest in the jet.

However, this is in the context of deeper Spanish and Turkish military-industrial cooperation.

While the outcome of the competition remains uncertain, the RAF’s requirement is likely to be shaped by a combination of training capability, programme risk, industrial participation and value for money. W

ith Hawk retirement approaching in the next decade, the eventual winner will not only become the RAF’s next advanced jet trainer but could also take on one of British aviation’s most visible roles as the aircraft of the Red Arrows.

The post JetBlue launches child-free flight, while easyJet helps fund babies’ passports appeared first on AGN.

]]> Parents and adults seeking a child-free getaway have a new option. JetBlue Vacations has teamed up with Virgin Voyages to pair a dedicated kids-free flight with an adults-only cruise.

Meanwhile, easyJet is taking a family-friendly approach, offering eligible parents a £66.50 contribution towards their baby’s first passport when booking their next easyJet holiday.

JetBlue and Virgin Voyages introduce adults-only travel

Dubbed “Do Not Disturb”, the new package from JetBlue Vacations and Virgin Voyages has been designed exclusively for travellers aged 18 and over.

The four-day package combines child-free round-trip JetBlue flights with a Virgin Voyages cruise and includes VIP experiences and optional add-ons throughout the holiday.

The package costs US$2,750 for two travellers and includes flights from New York’s JFK Airport to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Florida, as well as the cruise.

“People have wanted this kind of kid-free experience from take-off to sail away for a long time and now it actually exists,” said Nirmal Saverimuttu, CEO of Virgin Voyages.

Jamie Perry, President of Paisly, which powers JetBlue Vacations, said the collaboration was designed to deliver an adults-only experience from start to finish.

JetBlue wins $58.5m deal for Spirit’s New York slots after failed takeover JetBlue wins $58.5m deal for Spirit’s New York slots after failed takeover

“From the flight to the transfer to the cruise itself, we’ve thought about the entire journey so our customers can simply show up, settle in and enjoy some uninterrupted time away.”

Have other airlines introduced child-free flying?

While dedicated adults-only flights remain unusual, several airlines have introduced designated cabin areas aimed at passengers seeking a quieter journey.

In 2023, Corendon Dutch Airlines introduced an “only adults” zone for passengers aged 16 and over on selected Amsterdam-Curaçao flights.

In 2013, AirAsia X introduced a designated quiet section with age restrictions (passengers aged 12 and above) on selected A330 long-haul services. Singapore-based low-cost carrier Scoot also launched its “Scootinsilence” cabin on selected 787 flights for passengers seeking a more peaceful travel experience.

easyJet’s offer to help cover babies’ first passport costs

While JetBlue is targeting adults looking for a child-free escape, easyJet is offering a £66.50 credit towards a future easyJet holiday for eligible families, equivalent to the cost of a baby’s first passport.

The offer applies to infants under the age of two, and parents must book before 27 November.

Family travel is on the rise

According to easyJet, around 585,000 families welcome a new baby each year in England and Wales, and infants travelling this year have increased by 10% compared to 2025, with 22,000 more infants flying across its network in 2026.

City break bookings have seen a notable boost among young families, the carrier said.

The airline’s initiative to cover passport fees addresses practical and financial hurdles parents face when planning their first trip with a baby.

easyJet’s research shows that while almost 4 in 5 parents surveyed (82%) described their baby’s first holiday as a landmark moment, over a third (36%) identified the first passport photo as one of the biggest challenges to getting there.

“Travel has a unique way of bringing families together,” said Stuart Wright, Customer Director at easyJet holidays.

“A baby’s first holiday is often one of those moments parents remember for years to come. By covering the cost of a baby’s first passport, we’re helping more families start making those memories that little bit sooner.”

easyJet and easyJet holidays launch 15 new routes from Birmingham (United Kingdom) easyJet and easyJet holidays launch 15 new routes from Birmingham (United Kingdom)

Majority of families confident to travel with children

Underlining that family travel is on the rise, easyJet’s research also suggests that parents may find travelling with an infant less daunting than first anticipated. Almost half of respondents (48%) said a holiday with a baby in tow was easier than they had anticipated, while 78% said they would confidently do it again.

easyJet Captain Kate West, who is herself navigating new parenthood, said the initiative is intended to make travel more accessible for families.

 “We carry millions of families across Europe every year,” she said.

“We want to make travel as easy and accessible as possible for everyone, including young families. We hope that covering the cost of a baby’s first passport goes a small way towards making a family’s adventure a little easier and gives our youngest travellers a warm welcome to the world.”

]]> Artemis II crew faced cabin leak scare minutes before crucial Moon burn https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/artemis-ii-cabin-leak-scare/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:29:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54373 Artemis II pilot Victor Glover reveals how a false cabin leak warning nearly disrupted NASA’s historic Moon mission before its record-breaking journey.

The post Artemis II crew faced cabin leak scare minutes before crucial Moon burn appeared first on AGN.

]]>

NASA’s Artemis II astronauts received a suspected cabin leak warning just 15 minutes before a critical engine firing that would send them towards the Moon, raising the possibility that their historic mission could be cut short before it had even left Earth’s vicinity.

The incident, which occurred on 2 April this year, was disclosed by Artemis II pilot Victor Glover during a discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife on 18 October.

The warning came as the Orion spacecraft approached the lowest point of its elongated orbit around Earth, preparing for the manoeuvre that would commit its four astronauts to a journey around the Moon.

“If it had happened five minutes later, we may not have been able to have that burn,” Glover told the audience, according to Space.com.

The crew and mission controllers had to establish whether the warning indicated a genuine loss of cabin pressure. A real leak could have forced the astronauts to abandon their lunar journey, put on their spacesuits and prepare for an early return to Earth.

The warning was eventually determined to be false, allowing Orion to complete its engine firing and begin a journey that would carry humans further from Earth than ever before.

A warning at the worst possible moment

Artemis II had launched on 1 April aboard NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, carrying commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Glover, mission specialist Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen.

Rather than heading directly for the Moon, Orion first entered a highly elliptical orbit around Earth. The trajectory gave the astronauts and flight controllers time to check the spacecraft’s life-support systems, communications and handling before committing to deep space.

By 2 April, Orion had travelled roughly 38,000 miles from Earth and was returning towards the planet for its planned translunar injection burn.

The manoeuvre was timed to take place near the spacecraft’s closest approach to Earth, at an altitude of about 100 miles. 

At that point, Orion was travelling rapidly, making it an efficient place to fire the engine and gain the additional speed needed for the lunar journey.

Glover recalled Hansen looking through the window as Earth grew closer beneath them.

“I think we’re going to run smack dab into the middle of Earth,” Hansen remarked, according to Glover’s account reported by Space.com.

The crew also had to contend with an environment containing more orbital debris and satellites as Orion descended towards its lowest altitude.

Then came the cabin leak alert.

Determining whether the warning was genuine became an immediate priority. The astronauts could not ignore a possible loss of cabin pressure, but delaying the engine firing could also mean missing the planned opportunity to head towards the Moon.

NASA flight director Judd Frieling subsequently confirmed during an April briefing that the alert had been a false alarm.

A record-breaking journey beyond the Moon

The successful burn began a mission that would take the four astronauts farther from Earth than any previous human crew, surpassing the record established by Apollo 13 in 1970.

As Aerospace Global News reported following Orion’s safe return, the spacecraft reached a maximum distance of 252,756 miles from Earth, exceeding Apollo 13’s record by more than 4,000 miles.

During the lunar flyby on 6 April, Orion passed approximately 4,067 miles above the Moon’s surface. The astronauts photographed the lunar landscape and carried out observations intended to support future exploration.

Over the nearly 10-day mission, Orion travelled more than 694,000 miles, completing life-support checks, spacecraft handling exercises and scientific investigations.

The mission also marked the first time humans had travelled beyond low Earth orbit since the Apollo programme ended in 1972.

Artemis II was not designed to land on the Moon. Its primary purpose was to demonstrate that Orion and its supporting systems could safely carry astronauts into deep space and bring them home.

A major contribution came from the European Space Agency’s European Service Module, built under ESA leadership and largely assembled by Airbus Defence and Space in Bremen. It supplied propulsion, electrical power, air, water and thermal control during the flight.

The module performed with sufficient precision that two planned trajectory correction burns were no longer needed, according to ESA officials.

Orion’s return clears the way for future missions

Artemis II concluded on 10 April when Orion splashed down in the Pacific Ocean off San Diego, completing NASA’s first crewed lunar mission in more than half a century.

The spacecraft endured temperatures of approximately 5,000°F during atmospheric re-entry, followed by a planned communications blackout lasting just over six minutes. Its parachutes then deployed successfully, bringing the crew safely to the ocean.

The cabin leak warning, now described publicly by Glover, offers a reminder of how easily the mission’s outcome might have changed.

Artemis II went on to break the record for the greatest distance travelled from Earth by humans before returning safely on 10 April. 

The incident also showed why NASA had taken the precaution of checking Orion’s critical systems in Earth orbit before sending four astronauts on their journey around the Moon.

]]> Airport fees still outweigh fuel costs for Eurowings despite Middle East crisis https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/eurowings-airport-airline-fees-fuel-costs-middle-east-crisis/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 14:02:29 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54349 Rising fuel prices may dominate aviation headlines, but Eurowings says airport fees, taxes and charges remain an even bigger obstacle to keeping flights affordable and maintaining winter routes.

The post Airport fees still outweigh fuel costs for Eurowings despite Middle East crisis appeared first on AGN.

]]> Airport fees and charges remain a bigger cost burden for Eurowings than fuel, even as the Middle East crisis drives up Jet A-1 prices and disrupts supply, the German airline has said.

Speaking at Routes World 2026 in Frankfurt, Tobias Bracht, head of network and airport relations at the low-cost carrier, said airport charges and government-imposed fees comprised a large slice of the airline’s cost base and therefore were key factors in determining which routes airlines could sustain through a winter season.

Fees and charges outweigh fuel costs

Since the outbreak of war between the US and Iran in the spring of this year, the price of jet fuel surged and the focus has been on how airlines and their balance sheets will weather the storm. 

But while the fuel price is undoubtedly a concern for carriers, Bracht highlighted how fees and charges remained a significant burden – one that surpassed fuel even in the current high-cost environment. 

“We are all talking about … fuel, but even in today’s really high cost fuel environment, the fees and charges part is still significantly larger than fuel costs,” he said. 

That is particularly relevant for Eurowings, since the cost burden for carriers operating in Germany is higher than in other European countries.

Winter flying brings its own cost challenges

Looking ahead to the winter schedule, which begins on Sunday, these fees often continue to be levied even when demand drops off and revenue falls.

Bracht added that airlines were increasingly focused on whether winter flights could cover their variable costs, such as taxes, fuel and variable salaries for crew, rather than whether they could generate a positive earnings contribution once all the fixed costs were included.

“We have already incorporated and accepted that the flight itself will not make a positive EBIT from itself, but we rather see it as a marginal contribution towards the total year result, so that the summer doesn’t have to carry the total cost burden of winter.”

Bracht said roughly two thirds of his airline’s total costs were variable, with fees and charges accounting for about half of that portion.

In Germany, he said, government charges and airport costs each accounted for approximately half of the fees-and-charges category.

However, it is fuel that has attracted more of the attention, with the US-Iran conflict continuing to create uncertainty for airlines over energy prices, supply and operations. 

Airport fees and taxes remain a more substantial cost consideration for airlines such as Eurowings, even under the current fuel-market conditions – not least since fuel prices can fluctuate with global market conditions, while airport fees, passenger taxes and other government charges are often fixed, even during periods when demand and revenue are weaker.

Seasonal flexibility could support winter flying

Speaking to delegates at the event, the head of network urged governments and airports to look at the cost structure and consider lowering fees for off-season flights when demand and revenue is much lower. 

Bracht said the ability to reduce costs during the winter was complicated by the different approaches taken by governments and airports.

“Where it gets really, really tough is, of course, on the government side, where governments might take a more holistic approach and don’t care as much about seasonality.”

Many airports served by Eurowings continue to apply broadly uniform fees and charges throughout the year, regardless of the seasonal differences in airline demand.

Some airports, however, have begun to introduce greater flexibility, charging airlines more during the busier summer season while reducing charges during winter.

“This is a step towards bringing more flights in the winter,” he said.

The post Civil Air Patrol orders 21 Cessna aircraft to strengthen emergency response and training capabilities appeared first on AGN.

]]> Textron Aviation expects to deliver all 21 aircraft by year-end, bolstering the Civil Air Patrol (CAP) mission readiness as the US Air Force’s civilian auxiliary.

CAP’s order for 21 piston aircraft includes seven Cessna Skyhawk 172s, 11 Cessna Skylane 182s, two Cessna Turbo Skylane T182Ts, and one Cessna Turbo Stationair HD 206.

What is CAP and how does it support the US Air Force?

A volunteer organisation operating under the US Air Force as a civilian auxiliary, CAP supports military, civil and government agencies nationwide. The world’s largest operator of Cessna aircraft, CAP’s missions include military training and operations, as well as search-and-rescue work. It is also a youth development organisation supporting communities and young cadets who join as young as the age of 12 to adult volunteers.

The additional 21 Cessna piston aircraft ordered from Textron Aviation will boost CAP’s existing fleet of 543 single-engine aircraft (primarily Cessna aircraft and a selection of gliders) and help ensure its members are ready to respond as and when needed.

Major General Regena Aye, national commander and CEO of Civil Air Patrol, explained missions could involve “searching for someone who is missing, responding after a disaster, or introducing young people to aviation.”

The patrol has 72,000 members, including 35,000 adults and 37,000 youth, operating from more than 1,400 locations. While it is an auxiliary of the Air Force, CAP is not part of the military, and its members do not engage in combat. They do, however, work closely with the military and other government agencies to support the nation, particularly in times of crisis.

Since October 2024, CAP has flown nearly 200,000 hours, completed 860 search-and-rescue missions, and saved 104 lives. As a nonprofit organisation, it reported an estimated US$334 million in operational value on US$73.5 million in federal investments in early 2026. This represents more than US$4.50 in value for every federal dollar invested for the prior year.

Civil Air Patrol: The world’s largest fleet of Cessna aircraft is getting even bigger Civil Air Patrol: The world’s largest fleet of Cessna aircraft is getting even bigger

CAP’s order builds on existing relationship with Textron Aviation

The order for 21 additional aircraft builds on CAP’s long-standing partnership with Textron Aviation.

“Civil Air Patrol has a remarkable ability to turn flight hours into real impact for communities across the country,” said Bob Gibbs, vice president, Defense & Special Mission Sales, Textron Aviation.

The company’s aviation solutions provide the high-performance characteristics required to address the unique challenges of special operations. Its products offer low operating costs, reliability, and versatility, making them ideally suited for ambulance, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions, as well as utility transport and training.

“From search and rescue to disaster response and aviation education, these missions demand aircraft that are capable, dependable and ready to serve,” added Gibbs. “We’re proud that Cessna aircraft continue to play a role in helping CAP fulfill that mission.”

Why are Cessna aircraft so well suited to CAP’s missions?

With its diverse mission set, CAP’s fleet supports a wide range of operations, including search and rescue, disaster relief, and cadet orientation flights. All powered aircraft are equipped with modern avionics systems such as the Garmin G1000 and 3X Touch, providing pilots with enhanced situational awareness and navigation capabilities, making them essential for mission safety.

Known for its stability and ease of operation, the Cessna 172 is a four-seat, single-engine, high-wing aircraft. It is often deployed for cadet orientation flights, training, and search and rescue missions.

Like the Cessna 172, the 182 Skylane offers greater power and payload capacity, with a larger cabin. Often equipped with advanced avionics, it is typically used for longer-range missions, including aerial photography, disaster response, and transport.

Meanwhile, the larger six-seat Cessna 206 Stationair is used for missions requiring more cargo capacity and longer endurance. Its high-wing design and powerful engine make it suitable for various missions, including aerial photography and remote-area flying.

Several glider aircraft are also used for training in the cadet programme to introduce young members to aviation and basic pilot training. CAP has also begun integrating uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) in its operations.

]]> World’s first “sharkskin” Airbus A330 takes to the skies on passenger flights https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/worlds-first-sharkskin-airbus-a330-passenger-flights/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 12:06:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54337 Discover Airlines has introduced the world's first Airbus A330 fitted with AeroSHARK sharkskin technology into passenger service, cutting fuel burn and emissions.

The post World’s first “sharkskin” Airbus A330 takes to the skies on passenger flights appeared first on AGN.

]]> Discover Airlines has become the first airline to operate an Airbus A330 fitted with AeroSHARK, a sharkskin-inspired surface film that reduces aerodynamic drag and fuel consumption.

The Lufthansa Group leisure carrier introduced the modified Airbus A330-300, registered D-AIKP, into scheduled passenger service on 15 October, with a flight to Florida.

The aircraft underwent modification at Dresden Airport in late August, followed by several weeks of testing to assess the film’s performance during flight.

According to Discover Airlines, the tests confirmed that the technology could be used safely and reliably in regular airline operations.

The modification is expected to reduce the aircraft’s fuel consumption and associated carbon dioxide emissions by approximately 1%.

How does sharkskin technology work on aircraft?

AeroSHARK is a transparent adhesive film developed by Lufthansa Technik and Surventis (formerly BASF Coatings).

The film contains microscopic grooves, known as riblets, which imitate the structure of sharkskin. These grooves reduce friction between the aircraft’s surface and the surrounding airflow. Each riblet is about 50 micrometres high and aligned with the airflow.

On the Discover Airlines A330, the film has been applied to sections of the fuselage and engine nacelles.

By reducing frictional drag, the coating allows the aircraft to fly with slightly less engine thrust, lowering fuel consumption.

The technology can be installed on existing aircraft without replacing engines or making major structural modifications.

A 1% reduction in fuel consumption represents a relatively small saving on an individual flight. However, the savings accumulate over an aircraft’s operating life, particularly on long-haul routes.

Discover Airlines introduces AeroSHARK to Airbus operations

The Discover Airlines A330 is the first Airbus aircraft to enter scheduled passenger service with a large-scale AeroSHARK modification.

The airline worked with Lufthansa Technik and other partners on the installation and testing programme.

“With D-AIKP, we have not only added our first AeroSHARK-equipped aircraft to the fleet, but also reached an important milestone: For the first time, an Airbus with AeroSHARK modification is operating in regular scheduled service,” said Sascha Unterbarnscheidt, chief operating officer at Discover Airlines.

Discover Airlines operates leisure flights from Frankfurt and Munich to destinations across Europe and on long-haul routes.

The modified aircraft has returned to normal passenger service after completing flight testing.

Mastercard is also supporting the current development phase through a sustainability partnership with the Lufthansa Group.

Lufthansa Group already uses AeroSHARK on Boeing 777 aircraft

Although this is the first Airbus to enter passenger service with AeroSHARK, the technology is already used on Boeing 777 aircraft.

Lufthansa Technik first developed the modification for the Boeing 777 and later secured approvals covering the 777-300ER, 777-200ER and 777 Freighter.

SWISS, Lufthansa Cargo and Austrian Airlines are among the operators using the technology.

By September 2026, 23 Lufthansa Group aircraft had been fitted with AeroSHARK.

According to Lufthansa Technik, these aircraft collectively save more than 20 tonnes of jet fuel each day, avoiding approximately 64 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions.

At that rate, the annual savings would exceed 7,300 tonnes of fuel and approximately 23,000 tonnes of CO₂.

The actual savings depend on aircraft utilisation, flight distances and operating conditions.

AeroSHARK has also attracted interest from airlines outside the Lufthansa Group seeking ways to reduce fuel costs and emissions from aircraft already in service.

Airbus A330 approval could lead to wider adoption

Lufthansa Technik has been working with the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) on supplemental type certification for the Airbus A330-200 and A330-300.

As AGN reported in September, the company entered the final certification phase in late August, using the Discover Airlines aircraft for testing.

The programme involves technical assessments, flight testing and documentation to establish that the modification meets aviation safety requirements.

The A330 is an important aircraft type for the project because large numbers remain in commercial service worldwide. Lufthansa Technik previously estimated that approximately 1,000 A330-200 and A330-300 aircraft were operating globally.

Certification would allow the technology to be offered more widely to airlines operating these aircraft, subject to the applicable approval conditions.

Lufthansa Technik and Airbus are also working together to investigate applying AeroSHARK to additional aircraft surfaces, including the wings and horizontal and vertical stabilisers.

The companies estimate that expanding the area covered by AeroSHARK could increase fuel savings to more than 2% on typical long-haul flights.

Further testing and regulatory approvals will be required before those modifications can enter commercial service.

]]> Pentagon backs futuristic blended-wing aircraft that could transform military cargo flights https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/us-air-force-funds-natilus-kona/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 10:38:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54306 The US Air Force is funding multiple blended-wing-body aircraft projects as it evaluates new approaches to cargo transport and aerial refuelling.

The post Pentagon backs futuristic blended-wing aircraft that could transform military cargo flights appeared first on AGN.

]]> Blended-wing-body aircraft have long promised substantial efficiency gains over conventional designs.

Now, the United States Air Force is investing in two separate programmes, led by Natilus and JetZero, to assess whether the technology can help meet future cargo and tanker requirements in contested environments.

Natilus has previously told AGN that it is aiming for the first flight of a full-scale Kona prototype in 2027 or early 2028.

US Air Force invests in demonstrator for Natilus’ KONA BWB

Natilus has received $3.5 million in Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation (RDT&E) funding to develop a blended-wing body aircraft for the US Air Force.

The funding is to help accelerate the development of Natilus’s 3.8-ton payload optionally piloted KONA regional freighter toward a full-scale flight demonstrator.

The initial focus is to demonstrate KONA as a right-sized distribution platform for intra-theater lift and contested logistics.

The blended wing body (BWB) KONA sits between light utility aircraft like the C-208 and larger tactical airlifters such as the C-130. It has the potential to fill the gap with a new class of sub-tactical lift.

Currently, the primary military mission set for KONA is regional airlift. However, it is being designed with modular architecture and could be developed for other missions over time, including communications relay, ISR, and payload delivery.

Natilus CEO Aleksey Matyushev said, “With KONA, the Department of War is evaluating a new airlift capability that can generate real-world cost, reliability, payload and utilization data as the broader military requirement matures.”

Why the Air Force wants new forward cargo solutions in Indo-Pacific

KONA is being designed for a range of 800 nautical miles and is designed to operate on short runways intended for regional distribution and contested environments. In a future high-end war in the Indo-Pacific, forward runways are expected to be targeted and may be out of action.

The Air Force and other service branches are interested in a range of short-runway, or runway-independent solutions for the “last mile” of logistical support in the Indo-Pacific.

Blended wing designs offer the potential to significantly lower fuel burn, with Natilus saying its KONA will be able to achieve around a 30% improvement compared with comparable conventional aircraft.

For the Air Force, this offers reduced logistical strain in forward-deployed fuel, improved range, and frees up more of its payload capacity.

Natilus is currently advancing KONA toward FAA Part 23 certification and full-scale flight testing.

How Natilus redesigned Horizon to make blended wing body aircraft work for airlines How Natilus redesigned Horizon to make blended wing body aircraft work for airlines

Emerging Natilus and JetZero blended wing bodies

KONA is not the only next-generation BWB aircraft the Air Force is investing in. JetZero is currently working with Northrop Grumman with Air Force funding to develop the much larger Z4 blended wing body aircraft.

In the commercial sector, the Z4 would occupy a mid-sized airplane segment, roughly that of the Boeing 757/767. In the military sector, it has the potential to be a much larger transport aircraft and an aerial refueling tanker.

Both Natilus and JetZero see dual miltiary and commercial applications for their aircraft. JetZero’s investors include United Airlines and Alaska Airlines.

Natilus is developing a family of BWB aircraft. It claims to have accumulated 570+ aircraft pre-orders valued at $24 billion. Besides reducing fuel consumption by 30%, it aims for the aircraft to reduce operational costs by 50% and increase payload capacity by 40%.

]]> Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport is officially open, but international flights remain far from normal.

Aircraft operators must still obtain prior permission to land or depart, while many airlines continue to cancel services despite the airport’s reopening.

The restrictions, introduced after missile and drone attacks on the Saudi capital, have left passengers facing ongoing uncertainty. Although some flights remain on published schedules, airlines are still assessing operational and security risks.

There is no confirmed date for a full return to unrestricted international passenger services.

Flight-tracking service Flightradar24 reports that Riyadh airport is open to traffic subject to prior permission, but that no passenger flight had sought authorisation at the time of its update.

Riyadh Airport is open to traffic with prior permission, but so far no passenger flight has sought that permission. Since reopening, only private and cargo flights have operated at RUH. https://t.co/qdT3aOyLdf https://t.co/2tpJnkNmJz

— Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) October 20, 2026

As of this morning, Flightradar24 still showed King Khalid International as the world’s most disrupted airport, with a disruption index of 5.0, 180 cancelled flights and 3 delayed flights.

The only commercial airlines listed as operating for departures and arrivals were Saudia and flynas, though the schedule listing alone does not guarantee the flight will operate.

Riyadh Airport reopens under restrictions

The airport reopened on 18 October after more than a week of disruption. However, scheduled passenger services have not returned to normal, and international airlines continue to cancel flights to the Saudi capital.

Under NOTAM A3650/26, aircraft operators must obtain prior permission from Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) for arrivals and departures. A separate notice, A3651/26, prevents airlines from planning to use Riyadh as a diversion airport.

Both restrictions took effect on 17 October and have no specified expiry date.

Although some passenger flights still appear on published schedules, their presence does not confirm they have operated. Airlines including Lufthansa, KLM and Philippine Airlines have extended cancellations into November.

The airport’s restricted reopening offers little certainty to passengers waiting for regular commercial services to resume.

Which airlines are still cancelling Riyadh flights?

Several international carriers have announced cancellations extending well beyond the airport’s reopening. 

According to the airlines’ published advisories, Lufthansa has suspended Riyadh services through 18 November, while KLM has cancelled Riyadh and Dammam flights through 31 October.

Philippine Airlines has suspended its Riyadh services until 29 November. Cathay Pacific has postponed its planned return to Riyadh until the end of January 2027.

Qatar Airways and Etihad Airways have also extended cancellations affecting Riyadh and Dammam through 24 October.

Delta Air Lines postponed the launch of its new Atlanta-Riyadh service, originally scheduled for 23 October, until March 2027. 

Why are airlines not returning to Riyadh?

The restrictions follow repeated missile and drone attacks on the Saudi capital, including strikes that damaged airport facilities and commercial aircraft.

Security concerns extend beyond the airport to the airspace itself.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) has advised operators to avoid designated areas of Saudi airspace and exercise caution elsewhere because of missile and drone activity, air defence operations and the risk of aircraft being misidentified.

The US Federal Aviation Administration has issued a separate advisory urging caution over Saudi Arabia because of military activity and interference with satellite navigation systems.

These warnings do not prohibit every flight to Saudi Arabia. Airlines must assess the risks before deciding whether to resume services.

As AGN has previously reported, six commercial aircraft were damaged during the attacks, with a combined insured value of approximately $375 million, according to an insurance report reviewed by The Wall Street Journal.

What should passengers travelling to Riyadh do?

Passengers should not assume that an existing booking means their flight will operate.

Airlines may continue cancelling or rescheduling flights even while the airport remains officially open. Travellers should check their flight status directly with their airline before leaving for the airport.

Passengers whose flights have been cancelled should contact their airline or travel agent about alternative arrangements, rebooking and refunds.

The airport remains available to authorised aircraft movements, but there is no confirmed date for the restoration of unrestricted scheduled passenger operations.

]]> Air Astana’s first Boeing 787-9 begins flight testing ahead of 2027 debut https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/air-astana-first-boeing-787-9-flight-testing/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 09:16:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54300 Air Astana's first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner has entered flight testing in Charleston. The post Air Astana’s first Boeing 787-9 begins flight testing ahead of 2027 debut appeared first on AGN.

]]> Air Astana’s first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner has begun flight testing, bringing the Kazakh carrier closer to introducing a new long-haul fleet and launching nonstop services to North America.

The aircraft, registered EI-KZA, completed its first test flight on 1 October 2026 at Boeing’s Charleston manufacturing facility in South Carolina.

In an announcement posted on LinkedIn, Air Astana shared images from its factory flight-testing programme as Boeing completes the necessary certification and delivery procedures.

The airline expects its first three 787-9s to enter commercial service during 2027. The aircraft will replace its ageing Boeing 767-300ER fleet and support plans to expand its international network. 

Air Astana expects first Dreamliner delivery in December

Air Astana had originally expected to receive its first Dreamliner in September 2026, but manufacturing delays have pushed the anticipated handover to December.

Kazakhstan’s Vice Minister of Transport, Talgat Lastayev, confirmed the revised delivery schedule on 20 October.

The delay has also affected preparations for nonstop flights between Kazakhstan and the United States.

In an interview with Aviation Business News, Air Astana chief executive Ibrahim Canliel recently outlined a delivery schedule that would see the second Dreamliner arrive in January 2027 and the third in August 2027. He said the aircraft will initially operate about 20 regional sectors over two months to familiarise crews with the new type before entering longer-haul service.

The airline operates a fleet of 35 aircraft with an average age of 6.3 years, including three Boeing 767s and 33 Airbus A321s, Airbus A321neos, Airbus A321neo LR, Airbus A320ceos, and Airbus A320neos.

Air Astana introduced its Boeing 767-300ER aircraft in 2013. The airline plans to retire its Boeing 767-300ER aircraft progressively as the new Dreamliners enter operation.

The incoming Dreamliners will provide newer long-haul aircraft with improved fuel efficiency and additional range supporting new international routes.

The carrier also operates Airbus A321LR aircraft on long, thin international routes, allowing it to serve markets where demand would not justify widebody capacity.

New Boeing 787s will support US route plans

Air Astana has identified nonstop services to the US as a priority for its long-haul expansion.

Canliel said the carrier remains on course to introduce US flights during the second half of 2027, although the schedule depends on aircraft deliveries and operational approvals.

The airline is assessing polar routings and aircraft payload requirements to determine how it can operate the proposed services without intermediate fuel stops.

Kazakhstan’s transport authorities have also acknowledged that aircraft delivery delays are affecting preparations for direct flights.

The government has not confirmed a launch date or announced the specific US destinations it will serve.

The 787-9 offers substantially greater range than Air Astana’s existing 767-300ER fleet. The Boeing 767-300ER has a range of about 6,000 nautical miles, depending on payload and configuration. The Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner has a maximum published range of 8,300 nautical miles, allowing the airline to consider longer nonstop routes from Kazakhstan to North America and other international markets.

Air Astana could eventually operate 18 Boeing 787-9s

In November 2025, the airline announced an agreement with Boeing for up to 15 additional 787-9s. The order was finalised in February 2026 and includes five firm aircraft, five options and five purchase rights.

Combined with its earlier commitments, Air Astana could ultimately operate a fleet of 18 Dreamliners.

Deliveries under the additional order are planned between 2032 and 2035. The airline has estimated the combined value of the aircraft, including engines, at approximately $7 billion based on manufacturer list prices. 

The arrival of the first 787-9 will advance Air Astana’s plans to establish long-haul services and modernise its widebody fleet.

]]> IndiGo has extended its flight cancellations to Saudi Arabia, it announced today. The airline confirmed that services to Riyadh are now cancelled until 31 October. 

Meanwhile flights to and from Jeddah, Dammam and Madinah remain cancelled until 27 October.

The development comes as several international airlines approach the end of their announced suspension periods.

Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport reopened on 18 October after deadly missile and drone attacks on the Saudi capital forced it to close earlier in the month.

Although the airport has reopened, international flights remain severely disrupted. As we reported earlier this week, aircraft operators must still obtain prior permission to land or depart.

The restrictions have left passengers facing ongoing uncertainty. Although some flights remain on published schedules, airlines are still assessing operational and security risks.

IndiGo extends Riyadh flight cancellations until 31 October

IndiGo had previously given a cancellation deadline of 24 October. However in a post on X earlier today (23 October), IndiGo wrote: “The safety and well-being of our customers and crew remain our highest priority. We are closely monitoring developments and coordinating with the relevant authorities to assess the situation.”

Travel Advisory In view of the evolving security situation and following a careful assessment, IndiGo flights to and from Riyadh will remain cancelled until 31 October 2026 (inclusive), while flights to and from Jeddah, Dammam and Madinah will remain cancelled until 27 October 2026 (inclusive). The safety and well-being of our customers and crew remain our highest priority. We are closely monitoring developments and coordinating with the relevant authorities to assess the situation. Affected customers are being notified through the contact details provided at the time of booking. Customers are advised to check their flight status at https://t.co/m6CIGr4Vss before proceeding to the airport. We sincerely regret the inconvenience and uncertainty this may cause to your travel plans and appreciate your patience and understanding.

— IndiGo (@IndiGo6E) October 23, 2026

What should IndiGo passengers do?

In its post, the airline added: “Affected customers are being notified through the contact details provided at the time of booking. Customers are advised to check their flight status online before proceeding to the airport.”

Which airlines could restart Riyadh flights from 25 October?

Etihad Airways has confirmed flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh and Dammam will be cancelled until the end of the day on 24 October.

The airline has warned further changes are possible, and is advising customers to check before they travel.

Flydubai has also reportedly suspended flights to Riyadh, Dammam and Abha through 24 October.

Air India and Air India Express have announced cancellations affecting Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam until the same date, according to Reuters.

However, the expiry of a suspension period does not guarantee that flights will restart the following day.

Airlines must assess the security situation and obtain the necessary operating permissions before reinstating services.

Other airlines will not return to Riyadh until November or later

Some airlines are delaying their return until November, with some not planning to resume services in Riyadh until 2027.

Several international carriers have already confirmed longer suspensions, meaning Riyadh’s international network is unlikely to return to normal in the immediate future.

Reuters reported on 20 October that Air France-KLM had extended its Riyadh suspension until 7 November.

Lufthansa Group airlines have cancelled Riyadh flights until 18 November, while Philippine Airlines has suspended its services to the Saudi capital until 29 November.

Cathay Pacific has postponed the resumption of its Hong Kong–Riyadh route until the end of January 2027.

Delta Air Lines has also delayed the launch of its planned Atlanta–Riyadh service until March 2027. The US carrier had originally intended to begin operations on 23 October.

British Airways, meanwhile, has previously outlined plans to return with a limited Riyadh service from 3 November, although passengers should confirm whether those plans remain unchanged.

Is Riyadh airport open?

Yes. Saudi Arabia reopened King Khalid International Airport following safety inspections after the attacks earlier this month, but restrictions remain on airport operations.

Aircraft must still obtain prior approval before arriving or departing. The airport cannot currently be used as a planned diversion airport.

Why are airlines still cancelling flights after Riyadh airport reopened?

Under aviation notices issued following the closure, aircraft arriving at or departing from Riyadh require prior permission from Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation.

International airlines must consider the continuing risk of further attacks, operational restrictions and the availability of suitable alternative airports before restoring services.

The disruption has also affected other Saudi airports, with airlines cancelling flights to Dammam, Jeddah and Madinah.

Some services have returned. Malaysia Airlines resumed flights to Jeddah and Madinah on 18 October following a safety review, demonstrating that carriers are taking different approaches to restoring their Saudi networks.

What should passengers travelling to Riyadh do?

Passengers booked to travel to Riyadh from 25 October should check their flight status directly with the operating airline before leaving for the airport.

The coming weekend will be a key test for Riyadh’s aviation recovery, as airlines decide whether security conditions and operating restrictions allow flights to resume – or whether cancellations will extend further into November.
